title: What Can Language Models Inherit from Solomonoff Induction?Limits, Attainable Properties, and What Served Conditionals Reveal

paper.title: What Can Language Models Inherit from Solomonoff Induction? Limits, Attainable Properties, and What Served Conditionals Reveal
paper.abstract:
Abstract A familiar line of reasoning runs as follows: language models are flexible
approximators trained under a strictly proper loss, so scale brings them
closer to Solomonoff induction, and their predictive success is evidence of
that approach. We apply known results from algorithmic information theory,
universal prediction and Bayesian consistency. In its uniform form the
conclusion holds for no computable model: each has cheap environments it never
learns, and every uniformly computable family of total predictors shares one on
which each member fails beyond a horizon growing with its index, so “closer”
can hold only pointwise, one environment at a time. Nor could the offered routes
certify even that: finite
evaluation cannot certify agreement on rarely reached contexts, perfect
corpus fit selects the corpus law as prior, and asymptotic criteria cannot
see the constants that carry Solomonoff’s guarantee. Our lens is the Kraft
inequality read for predictors. Every model has at most the same budget of
predictive success, so Solomonoff’s predictor, which leaves part of it
unspent, differs from a language model not in having more of it but in where
it spends it; on mutually singular families
this is exact, and only full-mass Bayes mixtures reach the frontier. We
then discuss what is inheritable, including in-context learning as
amortised Bayesian inference; what survives within a context window; which
Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have or avoid; and what
served conditionals determine. A closing table states what common practices
certify and what to report. Tests are developed in a companion paper.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Language models are trained to minimise the log-loss, a strictly proper scoring rule [ 60 ] , and transformers are universal approximators of continuous sequence-to-sequence functions of fixed length on compact domains [ 203 ] . A familiar line of reasoning joins these facts: with enough data and compute, such a model approaches the predictor that learns every computable source, Solomonoff’s mixture over all computable hypotheses under a simplicity prior [ 172 , 173 ] , and its measured predictive success is evidence of that approach. We call this claim (C). Claim (C) is not a position anyone defends at full strength, and we do not attribute it to anyone. It is the common strengthening of a family of positions that are defended, stated at full strength so that the obstacles can be located: each obstacle below falls at a different point, and a claim held at half strength would hide which. The positions themselves are the target, and Figure 1 records for each one what survives and which result applies. The closest published statement of (C) itself, the hypothesis that transformers approximate Solomonoff induction better than any other extant sequence predictor [ 201 ] , is comparative and carries no guarantee. Deployed models, whose compute-efficient training stops well short of convergence [ 99 , 82 ] , give (C) little direct purchase. The weaker forms identify language modelling with compression [ 37 ] , whose efficiency is reported to track benchmark performance almost linearly [ 86 ] ; credit networks with a simplicity bias matched to real data [ 62 , 136 ] ; report that neural predictors meta-trained on samples from a universal prior show falling regret with scale on such samples, with convergence to Solomonoff’s predictor established in the limit under realisability rather than demonstrated [ 63 ] ; or describe language models as computable approximations to Solomonoff induction [ 188 ] . Each is a statement about where a model predicts well, and each survives this paper in part. What does not survive is the step they can be read as licensing: that the part which survives certifies the rest. None of the results below says that such success is no evidence at all about allocation elsewhere; they say that no finite amount of it can guarantee that allocation. Compression efficiency tracking benchmark performance is a statement about a corpus and bears on no other allocation (§ 5 ); a simplicity bias matched to real data is a statement about one prior and not about a universal one (§ 6 ); falling regret on samples from a universal prior is convergence under realisability , which is the hypothesis at issue (§ 4 ); and a computable approximation to Solomonoff induction is what Section 4 shows cannot be uniform. Figure 1 states this position by position.

sections.heading: The four positions, and what survives each.
sections.text: Compression. Language modelling is compression, and compression efficiency is reported to track capability [ 37 , 86 ] ; its most quoted informal statement in machine learning casts unsupervised learning as compression [ 177 ] . The position long predates that evidence. Compression on a fixed corpus was proposed as an objective replacement for the Turing test [ 127 ] , is the basis of a standing prize for compressing a snapshot of Wikipedia [ 90 ] , and was folded into formal intelligence measures by [ 76 , 77 ] ; the older form is the more specific one, because it names the corpus and so concedes what the recent form leaves open. A rate measures allocation on the data compressed , where universality costs at most K ⁡ ( q ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) K(q)+O(1) bits. What it does not do is certify a constant on a declared class: a rate below PNG or FLAC says nothing about one, and whether these models beat an adaptive low-order context model on the same chunks is not reported [ 37 , 78 ] . Compression by the shortest generated program, the reading closest to K K , remains far from strong baselines on real data [ 105 ] . Non-vacuous generalisation bounds do hold, on the training law and with prediction smoothing [ 122 , 123 ] . Survives as a statement about one corpus (§ 5 , Theorem 3.1 ). Simplicity bias. Networks prefer low-complexity functions and sequences, as real data do [ 62 , 136 ] . This is a direction of allocation, attainable and consistent with the no-free-lunch argument, and it is measurable as truth-loss levels on a declared class. What it is not is a universal prior, and asymptotic signatures cannot identify it (§ 6.1 , § 7 , Proposition 10.4 ). Meta-learned universal predictors. Neural predictors meta-trained on samples from a universal prior show falling regret with scale [ 63 ] , with convergence established in the limit under realisability rather than demonstrated. This is amortised Bayesian inference on the sampled class, certified in context by prior mass and exponentially weak in the task’s complexity. Outside the sampler’s bounds on program length and steps the prior is uncertified, and the network has its own diagonal environment (Proposition 6.1 , Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 ). Computable approximation. Training optimises program length through loss minimisation, and next-token prediction approximates Solomonoff induction better than other extant predictors [ 188 , 201 ] . The first reading is the K ⁡ ( q ) K(q) premium of § 5 : bounded and pathwise, but informative only where q q itself predicts well. The second survives as ε \varepsilon -optimality on a context distribution (Assumption 2.5 ), so that ranking predictors by closeness to Solomonoff’s means comparing constants on a declared class; convergence along a scaling family is pointwise, not uniform (Remark D.2 , § 4 with § C.4 , § 6 ). Figure 1: The four positions (C) strengthens, and the line each one stops at. The arrow is the boundary this paper draws: to its left, what the position establishes and this paper grants; to its right, the step it is commonly read as licensing and does not. The adjudication is in the text above, and the right-hand column names where each line is drawn.

sections.heading: The Kraft lens.
sections.text: For any predictor, computable or not, at most 2 b 2^{b} strings of a given length receive cumulative log-loss below b b bits. This is the Kraft inequality [ 107 , 129 ] read for predictors, a lens rather than a result: competence is a fixed budget. Solomonoff’s predictor has no more of it than a bigram model; it spends it elsewhere: within a factor 2 K ⁡ ( q ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) 2^{K(q)+O(1)} of what any computable q q spends on every sequence, which is what universality means. Where a predictor spends the budget is what its prior is. Each obstacle to (C) below is a statement about allocation; where the lens is exact is stated in Section 2.3 (Figure 2 ).

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: This is a discussion paper: most individual results are known, the dozen or so new pieces are mostly elementary, and Appendix H gives the role of each. The terrain it crosses has a standard survey in [ 156 ] , which treats universal induction as a theory of inference and asks whether it is the right formalisation of Occam’s razor. The scope here is narrower in two ways. It is about prediction and not about agency: the universal-agent programme that extends Solomonoff induction with a utility and an action channel is out of scope, and where a result from it is used (Pareto optimality among predictors in § 2.3 ), it is used for its prediction half only. And the question is empirical rather than foundational: not whether Solomonoff induction is the right ideal, but which of its properties a trained and served language model can have, which it cannot, and which of the routes commonly offered for the claim that it approaches one could establish it. Item (ii) shows that the conclusion of (C) in its uniform form holds for no computable model, and that approach can hold only pointwise, and items (i), (iii) and (v) that no route offered for it could certify it. (i) Evaluation (Section 3 ). Near-optimal expected log-loss bounds divergence on a set of contexts only in inverse proportion to its probability, so N N queries, adaptive or not, cannot separate models that differ only where the queries rarely go. Benchmark and red-team evidence can falsify, but never certify, agreement with a reference, and scaling curves track the ε \varepsilon of the test distribution only. (ii) Scale (Section 4 ). Putnam’s diagonal [ 152 ] , in Legg’s form [ 113 ] , gives every computable model, closed pipelines with chain of thought included, an environment no more complex than itself on which it loses log ⁡ V \log V bits per step ( log ⁡ ( 2 ​ V / 3 ) \log(2V/3) for real-valued conditionals) while Solomonoff’s predictor pays a constant (for tools and retrieval see Section 2.1 ). A uniformly computable family of total predictors shares one such environment; this forces nothing on a given model at an observable horizon, but shows that apparent convergence along a scaling family rests on replacing “one model that is good at every horizon” by “at every horizon, some model that is good”. (iii) Data (Section 5 ). A predictor with zero regret on its corpus coincides with the corpus law, so has finite regret only on sources absolutely continuous with respect to it, and at most log ⁡ c \log c on those it dominates by c c : fitting a corpus chooses a prior. Solomonoff’s predictor pays at most K ⁡ ( q ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) K(q)+O(1) bits more than it on the corpus, below one percent of the corpus code length at about 2 2 bits per token, 16 16 -bit weights and at least 10 3 10^{3} tokens per parameter. Data curation and mixture weights are prior design, and post-training reallocates under the same budget. (iv) Inheritance (Section 6 ). Solomonoff-form guarantees are attainable on declared classes by Bayes mixtures, the formal content of in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference. We state what a pretraining loss certifies about the in-context allocation, and why demonstrations can steer it. (v) Asymptotics (Section 7 ). Consistency, merging and vanishing per-step excess loss survive finite modification and reweighting of the prior [ 14 , 197 , 115 ] , while Solomonoff’s guarantee lives in the constants these operations change. Such criteria are blind to the prior. (vi) Deployment (Section 8 ). Within a context window, conservation, underdetermination, the single diagonal and prior reading keep their force. On stationary sources a bounded-window model repays the cost of identifying its environment at most about once per window, and exactly that on a copy source; only temperature one keeps Solomonoff’s bound; truncation is dogmatism by design; and the character-level law is a marginal over tokenisations. (vii) Properties (Section 9 ). We record which “Solomonoff-like” properties are attainable and, as a judgement, rank them; several attainable ones are attack surfaces, and we argue, without proof, that a trustworthy system should have Solomonoff-like beliefs and non-Solomonoff-like constraints. (viii) Measurement (Section 10 ). We define what served conditionals determine without a prior: a coherence residual and the arbitrage it prices, invariance nulls, and the implied prior over a declared class with its identifiability. The companion paper (Paper B) [ 210 ] turns them into tests and applies them to served models. Section 11 draws the consequences for research practice.

sections.heading: How to read this paper.
sections.text: Section 2 fixes notation and states the lens. Proofs are in the appendices, which open with a table of notation. Classical results are Facts, adapted or sharpened ones carry an “after” citation, and Appendix H records the status of each. Paragraphs headed “In words” restate key results. A shorter route for machine learning readers: Figure 1 , the Kraft lens (Section 2.2 and Figure 2 ), Sections 4 , 5 and 8 , and Table 2 . Resource-bounded forms of the limits are in Appendix I .

sections.heading: What is claimed and what is not.
sections.text: Nothing below shows that language models generalise poorly, that scale is unproductive, or that any particular system is deficient: no computable system has the universal property, so impossibility is not deficiency. Nor is attainability universality (a system matching a declared posterior exactly has its own diagonal environment), or uncertifiability unmeasurability (coherence, invariance and a prior over a declared class remain measurable). The claims concern what a class of arguments can establish and a class of measurements can certify, for idealised predictors at stated horizons, and Section 8 says which survive deployment. The paper measures no language model of its own; the served-model readings it relays in Section 11 are Paper B’s and are labelled as such. Its own computations are the worked numerical illustrations and the frontier figure, which are produced by the released scripts ( demo_paperA_numbers.py and fig_frontier.py ).

sections.heading: In words.
sections.text: Every predictor has the same fixed amount of predictive success to distribute over the strings of each length; predictors differ in where they put it and how much they leave unused, never in how much they have. On language models, accuracy on deterministic tasks tracks the probability of the output and of the task (rot-13 against rot-2), which is where the budget is spent [ 128 ] . The counting is that behind incompressibility; the correspondence between codes and priors it expresses underlies minimum description length and universal prediction [ 7 , 66 , 21 ] , and no-free-lunch results state the same trade for problems weighted uniformly [ 161 , 196 ] , which a simplicity prior escapes [ 111 ] . Whether that escape leaves the no-free-lunch theorems with any force against a learner that is doing well in practice is contested, and [ 174 ] argue the negative: the theorems presuppose learning algorithms that are purely data-driven, whereas standard algorithms take a model as input and can be given a model-relative justification, so the theorems constrain less than they are usually taken to. The counting used here does not depend on that dispute, and the difference is worth stating because the lens’s force rests on it. A no-free-lunch theorem averages performance over a weighting of problems and concludes that the average is fixed; change the weighting and the conclusion moves. The Kraft bound assumes no weighting at all. It says that on any antichain of strings (of one length, or any prefix-free set) at most 2 b 2^{b} members can be given loss below b b , because their probabilities must sum to at most one. That is a counting fact about the code, true of every predictor including M M , and it survives any reweighting of which problems matter. The simplicity prior escapes the average but not the ledger. Appendix A derives the exchange rate at which post-training and data mixtures reallocate: when q q is a measure, gaining b b bits on a set A A of strings of length n n removes at least ( 2 b − 1 ) ​ q ​ ( A ) (2^{b}-1)\,q(A) of mass from the rest (Corollary A.3 ). M M , a semimeasure that leaks (its measure part, Lemma B.1 , has mass below one, for otherwise M M would be a lower-semicomputable measure, hence computable, and could not dominate the point mass on its own diagonal sequence), spends less of the budget than a softmax language model, which spends all of it, and lies off the frontier of every pairwise singular family (Section 2.3 ); what separates them is where each spends (the last clause of Fact 2.4 ) and the diagonal constructions of Section 4 . At a finite horizon, and hence within any context window, the budget binds exactly on environments: if z ( 1 ) , … , z ( m ) z^{(1)},\dots,z^{(m)} have pairwise distinct length- n n prefixes, then ∑ k 2 − R n ​ ( q , z ( k ) ) ≤ 1 \sum_{k}2^{-R_{n}(q;z^{(k)})}\leq 1 , so at least half of them cost q q more than log ⁡ ( m / 2 ) \log(m/2) bits (the finite-horizon Kraft law, Corollary A.4 ). The same law caps the loss ceilings log ⁡ ( 1 / w h ) \log(1/w_{h}) that a Bayes mixture over deterministic hypotheses can promise on many tasks at once (the Kraft floor, Corollary A.5 ).

sections.heading: 2.3 The frontier of regret profiles
sections.text: Which regret profiles can one predictor achieve on a family, and which are best? For mutually singular environments, Kraft’s inequality answers. The theorem combines the Lebesgue decomposition and data processing with the distinguishability argument of [ 130 ] , the measure part of a semimeasure [ 118 , 13 ] , and Pareto optimality of Bayes mixtures [ 87 ] . Hutter proves that ξ \xi is Pareto-optimal, remarks that “for prediction only Bayes-mixes are Pareto-optimal”, and asks for the precise statement: “it would be interesting to show under which conditions, the class of all Bayes-mixtures (i.e. with all possible values for the weights) is complete in the sense that every Pareto-optimal strategy can be based on a Bayes-mixture” [ 87 , §5.2] . For finite families at a finite horizon, Wald’s complete-class theorem [ 186 ] already gives it (Proposition B.4 (i)). Clause (iii) gives it at R ∞ R_{\infty} for countable pairwise mutually singular families, where the full-mass Bayes mixtures are exactly the predictors whose Kraft sum is one; once the carriers are disjoint that equality is close to immediate, and what is added is the countable case, the ledger and its converse. The closest prior statement of the equality case we have found is an aside of Koolen’s [ 108 , §4.1] , whose subject is absolute loss: “For certain log loss games, each Pareto regret trade-off is witnessed uniquely by the Bayesian mixture of expert predictions w.r.t. a certain non-uniform prior and vice versa (not shown).” That is an unproved remark about expert games at finite horizon rather than about R ∞ R_{\infty} on mutually singular measures, and we have not found the ledger or the converse of Proposition B.2 stated anywhere.

sections.heading: Setting.
sections.text: The regret profile of q q on ℱ = ( μ k ) k ∈ J \mathcal{F}=(\mu_{k})_{k\in J} is ( R ∞ ​ ( q , μ k ) ) k ∈ J (R_{\infty}(q;\mu_{k}))_{k\in J} , and the Kraft set is 𝖪𝗋 J := { r ∈ [ 0 , ∞ ] J : ∑ k 2 − r k ≤ 1 } \mathsf{Kr}_{J}:=\{r\in[0,\infty]^{J}:\sum_{k}2^{-r_{k}}\leq 1\} with 2 − ∞ := 0 2^{-\infty}:=0 . Distinct deterministic environments, and distinct stationary ergodic measures, are mutually singular; two laws whose first-symbol marginals have full support and which agree thereafter are not. sections.heading: 3 What evaluation can certify
sections.text: Language models are evaluated on finite evidence. Benchmarks draw prompts from a fixed distribution, red teams choose prompts adaptively, and scaling studies fit held-out loss curves. Two elementary tools, Markov’s inequality and a coupling of evaluation runs, show what this evidence can establish. It constrains a model’s conditionals only on contexts that the evaluation reaches with probability comparable to the inverse of its number of queries. It can therefore falsify agreement with a reference such as Solomonoff’s predictor, but it cannot certify that agreement where agreement would matter. The intuition is old, from identification in the limit [ 61 ] and the no-free-lunch theorems [ 196 ] ; what follows makes it quantitative. Throughout, q q satisfies Assumption 2.5 with respect to ( μ , ρ ) (\mu,\rho) , and D ( c ) := D ( μ ( ⋅ ∣ c ) ∥ q ( ⋅ ∣ c ) ) D(c):=D\!\left(\mu(\cdot\mid c)\,\|\,q(\cdot\mid c)\right) .

sections.heading: In words.
sections.text: A good average score on a test distribution says almost nothing about the contexts that distribution rarely produces. On a set of small probability, a model’s predictions can be replaced at will at negligible cost to its average score. No test that samples contexts from the same distribution can tell the replaced model from the original. Clause (iii) covers any verdict computed from the observations at the queried contexts, including accuracy on single-symbol answers sampled from q q ; an answer of several symbols reads q q at contexts beyond the sampled one, which the clause covers only when those contexts are counted among the N N queries and B B is closed under the extensions read. Choosing conditionals on B B that put half their mass on a least likely symbol of a reference P ∗ P^{*} yields Corollary C.1 . Suppose q q satisfies Assumption 2.5 and passes a given N N -query evaluation with probability at least 1 − α 1-\alpha . Then some predictor q ′ q^{\prime} satisfies the assumption with ε + δ ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ V ) \varepsilon+\delta\log(2V) , passes with probability at least 1 − α − N ​ δ 1-\alpha-N\delta , and is at total-variation distance at least 1 2 − 1 2 ​ V \tfrac{1}{2}-\tfrac{1}{2V} from P ∗ P^{*} at every context of B B . Take P ∗ P^{*} to be the conditionals of M M . Empirical success under Assumption 2.5 then does not bound disagreement with Solomonoff’s predictor on any set of contexts whose ρ \rho -probability is small compared with 1 / N 1/N . The regime is not exotic: contexts of length below n n number ( V n − 1 ) / ( V − 1 ) (V^{n}-1)/(V-1) , while a corpus or benchmark touches a vanishing fraction of them.

sections.heading: 3.2 Adaptive evaluation
sections.text: An evaluator who chooses its N N contexts, adaptively and with full sight of the served conditionals, is not covered by Theorem 3.1 (iii), and the transcript-coupling argument familiar from query-complexity lower bounds says how much it can gain. Let ℛ δ := { c : ρ ⁡ ( c ) ≤ δ } \mathcal{R}_{\delta}:=\{c:\rho(c)\leq\delta\} be the individually rare contexts and ρ ¯ δ := ρ ⁡ ( ℛ δ ) \bar{\rho}_{\delta}:=\rho(\mathcal{R}_{\delta}) their total mass. Against any adaptive protocol, a predictor q ′ q^{\prime} that differs from q q only on a set B ⊆ ℛ δ B\subseteq\mathcal{R}_{\delta} of mass between δ \delta and 2 ​ δ 2\delta , and is far from any reference P ∗ P^{*} on all of B B , changes the verdict law by at most the query mass the protocol places on B B . A protocol that separates q q from every such q ′ q^{\prime} with error at most α \alpha on each side therefore needs N ≥ ( 1 − 2 ​ α ) ​ ρ ¯ δ 2 ​ δ N\;\geq\;(1-2\alpha)\,\frac{\bar{\rho}_{\delta}}{2\delta} queries, and passive sampling already reaches the matching order: it detects any fixed disagreement set of mass δ \delta with N ≥ ln ⁡ ( 1 / α ) / δ N\geq\ln(1/\alpha)/\delta queries.

sections.heading: What adaptivity buys.
sections.text: At a given resolution δ \delta , choosing where to look buys at most the factor 2 ​ ln ⁡ ( 1 / α ) / ( ( 1 − 2 ​ α ) ​ ρ ¯ δ ) 2\ln(1/\alpha)/((1-2\alpha)\bar{\rho}_{\delta}) over passive sampling (Theorem C.2 ). The comparison is at fixed δ \delta and presumes ρ ¯ δ ≥ δ \bar{\rho}_{\delta}\geq\delta : the factor is a constant when the rare mass is of order one at the resolution of interest, which holds for a corpus prefix law, and is not when the rare mass is itself of order δ \delta , as it is for a prompt law concentrated on a few items; since ρ ¯ δ ↓ 0 \bar{\rho}_{\delta}\downarrow 0 as δ ↓ 0 \delta\downarrow 0 , no factor is constant uniformly in δ \delta . The comparison is not quite like for like, and the asymmetry favours the passive side: the adaptive figure is a lower bound on separating q q from every q ′ q^{\prime} , while the passive one is an upper bound on separating a known P ∗ P^{*} , which for P ∗ = M P^{*}=M is never in hand. The factor is therefore a ceiling on what adaptivity can buy, not a measured exchange rate. A protocol published and fixed before the model is trained or tuned is the extreme case: a disagreement placed among the rare contexts it does not query is invisible to it. The restriction to individually rare contexts cannot be dropped, since fewer than 1 / δ 1/\delta contexts have probability above δ \delta and a protocol can query all of them. Nor can the bound be stated through ρ \rho ’s largest atom: if ρ \rho draws a position t ≤ n t\leq n uniformly and returns the prefix x < t x_{<t} , the empty context alone has mass 1 / n 1/n . What adaptivity does buy is the ability to find failures rather than wait to sample them. Section 4 shows that failures of a specific, cheaply constructed kind always exist: an adaptive evaluator can falsify, but it cannot certify.

sections.heading: Benchmarks, red teaming, scaling curves and contamination.
sections.text: These are instances of the same bound. Accuracy is a coarse function of the conditionals, so passing an accuracy benchmark is compatible with near-maximal disagreement with a reference on a set of small mass; red teaming falsifies but cannot certify; scaling laws measure the excess loss on the evaluation law and say nothing off it; and contamination changes which contexts the bound is about. Appendix C.2 works each out.

sections.heading: 4 What scale cannot deliver
sections.text: Scaling suggests a retreat from (C): no fixed model is Solomonoff’s predictor, but ever larger models approach it. Putnam’s classical diagonal argument [ 152 ] , in the complexity-theoretic form given by Legg [ 113 ] , implies that no computable predictor has Solomonoff’s regret property. A dovetailed form of the same argument applies to a whole uniformly computable family of total predictors at once. The family result has no force on any particular model at any observable horizon; what it shows is that the apparent convergence of scaling is a quantifier exchange. Sterkenburg [ 176 , 175 ] analyses the scope of the diagonal argument in detail.

sections.heading: 4.1 A single predictor
sections.text: Theorem 4.1 (Diagonal environment; after Putnam and Legg [ 152 , 113 ] ) . Let q q be a total rational-computable predictor. Define x q ∈ 𝒜 ∞ x^{q}\in\mathcal{A}^{\infty} by x t q := min ⁡ arg ​ min a ∈ 𝒜 ​ q ​ ( a ∣ x < t q ) x^{q}_{t}:=\min\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q(a\mid x^{q}_{<t}) , where the minimum is taken in a fixed order on 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , and let μ q \mu_{q} be the point measure on x q x^{q} . Then: (i) q ⁡ ( x t q ∣ x < t q ) ≤ 1 / V q(x^{q}_{t}\mid x^{q}_{<t})\leq 1/V for every t t , hence R n ( q ; μ q ) = L n ( q ; x 1 : n q ) ≥ n log V R_{n}(q;\mu_{q})=L_{n}(q;x^{q}_{1:n})\geq n\log V for all n n ; (ii) μ q \mu_{q} is computable with K ⁡ ( μ q ) ≤ K ⁡ ( q ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) K(\mu_{q})\leq K(q)+O(1) , and R n ​ ( M , μ q ) ≤ K ⁡ ( q ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) R_{n}(M;\mu_{q})\leq K(q)+O(1) for all n n . (Proof: Appendix C.3 .)

sections.heading: In words.
sections.text: Every fixed computable predictor has a computable sequence, no more complex than the predictor itself, on which it does no better than uniform guessing at every step. On the same sequence, Solomonoff’s predictor pays a constant in total. The construction extends to real-valued computable conditionals, with per-step loss at least log ⁡ ( 2 ​ V / 3 ) \log(2V/3) in place of log ⁡ V \log V . It therefore yields Corollary C.3 : no computable predictor has finite regret on every computable environment. This covers every language model taken as a closed pipeline (Definition 2.2 ), so the consequent of (C) holds for none, and empirical evidence can bear only on graded, class-relative versions of it (Section 6 ), where coverage itself has a price in description length [ 113 ] (Remark D.6 ). The diagonal environment is not one exotic sequence. Behind every prefix p p there is such an environment, of complexity at most K ⁡ ( p ) + K ⁡ ( q ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) K(p)+K(q)+O(1) , on which q q loses at least log ⁡ V \log V per step after p p . Behind the prefixes of length ℓ \ell there are V ℓ V^{\ell} distinct ones (Theorem C.6 ). At the step where the environment leaves p p , the loss is at least log ⁡ ( ( V − 1 ) / ( 1 − q max ) ) \log((V-1)/(1-q_{\max})) , where q max q_{\max} is the model’s largest conditional at p p , so it grows with sharpness. This is not a cost of scale: sharpness beyond calibration is documented after post-training (Section 5 ), while larger pretrained models are better calibrated on multiple-choice questions [ 95 ] . A user who can read the served conditionals, and who always continues with a least likely symbol, realises a finite-horizon instance of the construction (Remark C.5 ).

sections.heading: A model family.
sections.text: A scaling family generated by one program from an index is effectively enumerable, and a dovetailed form of the same construction gives a single environment on which every member of a uniformly computable family fails, member i i beyond a horizon growing with its index (Theorem C.7 , Appendix C.4 ). It forces nothing on any particular model at an observable horizon; what it shows is that the apparent convergence of scaling is a quantifier exchange. Computable families converging pointwise to M M exist; what fails is selection, since a rule that selects, ensembles or switches between members by any computable function of the data is one computable predictor with its own diagonal (§ C.4 ).

sections.heading: Randomised decoding.
sections.text: Served models sample, and serving can be nondeterministic across batches [ 72 ] . Randomisation does not evade the diagonal. If the scored object is the served conditional, as whenever log-probabilities are read, temperature and truncation are deterministic reshapings of it and Definition 2.2 applies unchanged. If instead the conditionals q ω ( ⋅ ∣ x ) q_{\omega}(\cdot\mid x) depend on internal randomness ω \omega , apply the construction to the mean predictor q avg ( ⋅ ∣ x ) := 𝔼 ω q ω ( ⋅ ∣ x ) q^{\mathrm{avg}}(\cdot\mid x):=\mathbb{E}_{\omega}q_{\omega}(\cdot\mid x) (not the measure part q ¯ \bar{q} of Section 2.3 ), which is computable whenever the seed law is. On the approximate diagonal of q avg q^{\mathrm{avg}} , Jensen’s inequality at each step gives 𝔼 ω L n ( q ω ; x 1 : n q avg ) ≥ n log ( 2 V / 3 ) \mathbb{E}_{\omega}L_{n}(q_{\omega};x^{q^{\mathrm{avg}}}_{1:n})\geq n\log(2V/3) , and that diagonal has complexity K ⁡ ( q avg ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) K(q^{\mathrm{avg}})+O(1) . The budget of Fact 2.6 belongs to the averaged allocation.

sections.heading: The resource-bounded form.
sections.text: Both diagonals have forms for models of bounded description length and per-step compute, in which the failing environment moves with the budget; Section 8 summarises them and Appendix I proves them.

sections.heading: 5 Fitting a corpus chooses a prior
sections.text: Carried to its limit, Assumption 2.5 delivers a predictor with zero excess loss over the corpus law. Minimising log-loss is minimising code length [ 29 , Ch. 5] , and strict propriety makes the source itself the unique minimiser of the population risk [ 60 ] . Fitting a corpus selects the corpus law as the prior. That prior has finite regret only on laws absolutely continuous with respect to it, and at most log ⁡ c \log c on a law it dominates by c c . The later training stages (data mixing, post-training, refitting on generated text) move the allocation around without enlarging the budget of Fact 2.6 .

u\ll\mu . Two readings of “the corpus law” must be kept apart. The empirical law of a finite corpus is atomic, so the second half of clause (iii) does not apply to it, though the first does. Its exact fit has infinite loss on every string of the corpus length that the corpus does not contain (Corollary E.4 (iv)). Memorisation studies measure how close trained models come to that extreme [ 47 , 18 ] . The theorem applies as stated to the population law. In both readings the law is over tokens, and the law over characters is a marginal over tokenisations (Section F.5 ). Clause (ii) is the constructive side. Clause (iv) says that no computable corpus carries every class’s constants, so the simplicity prior is not recovered by fitting a computable corpus and has to be supplied (Corollary D.1 ). It can be computed over a declared class, as in enumerated mixtures over programs up to a declared budget (companion work [ 49 , 20 ] ). Or it can be amortised, by pretraining on samples from such an enumeration [ 63 ] ; this extends reach but gives up the certificate (Theorem 3.1 ). At finite loss the closure is approached at a rate (Corollary E.2 (i)).

sections.heading: What the constant buys.
sections.text: By Fact 2.4 , for every computable model q q and every string x x of length n n , L n ​ ( M , x ) ≤ L n ​ ( q , x ) + K ⁡ ( q ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) L_{n}(M;x)\leq L_{n}(q;x)+K(q)+O(1) . The on-corpus premium of universality over a given model is therefore at most K ⁡ ( q ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) K(q)+O(1) bits, paid once, pathwise, at every horizon. K ⁡ ( q ) K(q) is at most the length of a program that stores the weights and runs inference, and prequential coding describes a trained network far more briefly than its stored weights [ 16 ] , so the figure below is conservative. For N par N_{\mathrm{par}} parameters stored at 16 16 bits, trained on N tok N_{\mathrm{tok}} tokens coded at b b bits per token, the premium is at most about 16 ​ N par / ( b ​ N tok ) 16N_{\mathrm{par}}/(b\,N_{\mathrm{tok}}) of the corpus code length. The 8-billion-parameter Llama 3 model saw about 1.5 × 10 13 1.5\times 10^{13} tokens, nearly 2 × 10 3 2\times 10^{3} per parameter [ 41 ] . With 16 16 -bit weights, at least 10 3 10^{3} tokens per parameter and b ≈ 2 b\approx 2 , the ratio is below one percent; for the 70-billion-parameter model, on the same token count (about 200 200 per parameter), it is about four percent, and at a few tens of tokens per parameter it would be a sizeable fraction. The premium is bounded and the reverse trade (clause (iii)) is not (Remark D.2 ). The compression view of language modelling [ 37 ] reaches the same accounting from the other side: once model size is charged, large models compress small datasets poorly, and that charge is the K ⁡ ( q ) K(q) premium above. A compression rate measured on one corpus measures allocation on that corpus (off-corpus rates: Section 11 ).

sections.heading: Post-training, data mixing and refitting.
sections.text: Post-training is a reallocation: at a fixed prompt, the exact optimiser of a KL-regularised reward objective changes the regret on each environment by an affine function of that environment’s mean reward, a price no KL budget bounds; doubling a source’s weight buys one bit on it and costs bits on the others; and maximum-likelihood refitting on generated data drifts to a vertex of the allocation. Appendix E.1 states these and relates them to the documented calibration and pass@ k k costs of post-training.

sections.heading: 6 What is inheritable
sections.text: This section collects what a computable predictor can inherit from Solomonoff induction. Pretraining sets an allocation, the context sets a posterior under it, and tools and test-time compute change the class over which the allocation is spread.

sections.heading: Class mixtures.
sections.text: Hutter’s mixture bound [ 87 , 89 ] is the answer on declared classes. Let 𝒞 = ( μ i ) \mathcal{C}=(\mu_{i}) be a uniformly computable family and w w a computable prior with w i > 0 w_{i}>0 , ∑ i w i ≤ 1 \sum_{i}w_{i}\leq 1 and computable tail bounds. Then the Bayes mixture ξ w \xi_{w} of ( 2 ) is computable, and R ∞ ​ ( ξ w , μ i ) ≤ log ⁡ ( 1 / w i ) R_{\infty}(\xi_{w};\mu_{i})\leq\log(1/w_{i}) for every i i (the mixture bound, Fact D.3 ), with equality on a singular family (Theorem 2.7 (ii)). Computable predictors thus attain the form of Fact 2.4 , with two substitutions: an enumerable class replaces the universal one, and log ⁡ ( 1 / w μ ) \log(1/w_{\mu}) replaces K ⁡ ( μ ) K(\mu) . The second substitution is forced: on any infinite uniformly computable family of distinct deterministic environments, no computable predictor has regret within a constant of K K (Proposition D.4 ). Only the universal class itself is excluded, by the diagonal of Section 4 . The standard predictors are rungs on this ladder, with their constants in Appendix D : the Krichevsky–Trofimov estimator [ 109 ] , context-tree weighting [ 194 ] , exhaustively enumerated bounded-program mixtures (companion work [ 49 ] ), and Levin search and the speed prior [ 116 , 163 ] .

sections.heading: The hierarchy is strict.
sections.text: Take any total rational-computable predictor q q and add its diagonal environment (Theorem 4.1 ) as a mixture of joint laws with a computable weight δ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \delta\in(0,1) . The result costs at most log ⁡ 1 1 − δ \log\frac{1}{1-\delta} on every source at every horizon. On the diagonal it has regret at most log ⁡ 1 δ \log\frac{1}{\delta} , where q q pays n ​ log ⁡ V n\log V (the non-collapse theorem, Theorem D.5 ). So no computable predictor is maximal or complete, and coverage of a whole class is priced by description length. A model’s inductive position is therefore a class together with constants on it, not a scalar degree of universality.

sections.heading: 6.1 In-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference
sections.text: On a class mixture, the conditional law after a context c c is ∑ k π ( k ∣ c ) μ k ( ⋅ ∣ c ) \sum_{k}\pi(k\mid c)\,\mu_{k}(\cdot\mid c) . Pretraining fixes the weights; the context moves the posterior. This is the formal content of the Bayesian reading of in-context learning [ 199 ] . It has been tested where the prior is known, and its nulls probed on pretrained models, where it is not. • Transformers meta-trained on sampled tasks approximate the posterior predictive [ 138 , 147 ] , and the error of the Bayes-optimal such predictor decomposes into a meta-learning and an intra-task term, both controlled by the mutual information between the task and the observed sequence [ 92 ] , the same quantity that carries the memory term of Proposition 8.1 . • Meta-training on conditionally i.i.d. tasks predicts exchangeable demonstrations [ 138 ] . Few-shot accuracy of pretrained models depends on demonstration order [ 124 ] and on majority-label and recency biases [ 205 ] , violations of the order null that exchangeable Bayes predictors satisfy (Proposition 10.3 ). • With few pretraining tasks, the model is Bayes-optimal for that discrete prior over seen tasks. Past a task-diversity threshold it departs from that Bayes predictor, even on the pretraining tasks, towards ridge regression, Bayes for a Gaussian prior, and so generalises to unseen tasks [ 157 ] : a small in-distribution excess buys a different allocation off the pretraining tasks, as Proposition 6.1 permits. • Falck et al. find violations of the martingale property, and detecting them requires no knowledge of the prior [ 46 ] ; Chlon et al. trace such martingale and order violations to positional encodings, which break exchangeability, and argue that they are compatible with Bayesian prediction in expectation over orderings [ 25 ] . • Min et al. find that replacing demonstration labels with random ones barely lowers accuracy on many classification tasks, while the label space, the input distribution and the format matter [ 134 ] . In the mixture reading, such demonstrations carry evidence mainly about which task is in play: Pan et al. separate this task recognition, which survives random labels, from task learning, which needs correct labels and emerges with scale [ 145 ] . Larger models override semantic priors when in-context labels are flipped [ 192 ] , a direct reading of prior strength against in-context evidence. A mechanistic line explains the same behaviour by the algorithm a forward pass runs. Transformers trained on simple function classes learn them in context [ 58 ] , and on linear regression their predictions track gradient descent or ridge regression, which a forward pass can implement [ 184 , 1 ] . The two readings agree on how a posterior can be computed but can disagree on which prior is held: when the implemented algorithm is Bayes for a prior other than the pretraining law, as past Raventós et al.’s diversity threshold, the mechanism, not the pretraining mixture, fixes the allocation. Whether in-context learning appears at all depends on properties of the data, such as burstiness and Zipfian class frequencies [ 22 ] , and it can be transient, giving way to in-weights learning under further training [ 168 ] . Wurgaft et al. model both the threshold and transience as Bayesian model selection between a memorising and a generalising predictor under a loss–complexity trade-off [ 198 ] : the allocation lens applied to predictors, with an explicit simplicity penalty, consistent with the K ⁡ ( q ) K(q) premium of Section 5 . As to which prior is held, parameter–function maps of small networks at initialisation favour simple functions [ 182 , 136 ] , and SGD approximately samples the Bayesian posterior under that prior [ 135 ] . Trained transformers prefer low-complexity sequences and hypotheses [ 62 , 38 ] . Meta-learning yields Bayes-optimal sequential strategies [ 142 ] , networks trained on samples from a universal mixture amortise it [ 63 ] , and the in-context objective is a prequential code length [ 44 ] . Each measures allocation on a finite family through a complexity proxy; none could certify constants on an unbounded class (Corollary C.1 ), and an amortised prior is underdetermined off its task-sampling law. What does a pretraining loss certify?

sections.heading: Setting.
In words.
sections.text: A pretraining loss certifies the Bayes constants of the pretraining prior, and it does so by prior mass, not task by task. An excess of ψ \psi bits per window leaves room to degrade all tasks in a set of prior mass about ψ / c ⁡ ( η ) \psi/c(\eta) by η \eta bits each. A single task of weight π k \pi_{k} can lose about 2 ​ ( 1 − π k ) ​ ψ / ( π k ​ ln ⁡ 2 ) \sqrt{2(1-\pi_{k})\psi/(\pi_{k}\ln 2)} bits while ψ ≪ π k \psi\ll\pi_{k} , and about ψ / π k \psi/\pi_{k} beyond that; at π k = 2 − 20 \pi_{k}=2^{-20} and ψ = 10 − 3 \psi=10^{-3} the first expression reads 55 55 bits against an exact certificate of 1050 1050 . Clause (i) is the log-loss form, with tight constants, of Zhang et al.’s bound [ 204 ] . That bound controls in-context regret by the Bayes-model-averaging regret plus a coverage constant γ cov \gamma_{\mathrm{cov}} , here 1 / λ 1/\lambda , times the pretraining error, so the dependence on the weight of the task is intrinsic. Wies et al. need a floor on component weights for the same reason [ 193 ] . The simpler bound ψ / c ⁡ ( η ) \psi/c(\eta) is tight only as the mass tends to zero. When inf k π k = 0 \inf_{k}\pi_{k}=0 , no rate holds uniformly over tasks (Corollary E.2 ). Clause (iii) is the exact price of specialisation at a finite horizon, and it needs disjoint supports. Generalisation beyond the pretraining tasks [ 157 ] relates to it only by analogy: those regression tasks carry Gaussian noise and overlap the pretraining law. Three limits apply. First, the task-mixture model of a corpus is an idealisation [ 199 ] , literal for prior-fitted networks, synthetic-task pretraining and amortised enumerations. Second, ψ \psi is cumulative over the window, not per token: a per-token excess ε = 10 − 3 \varepsilon=10^{-3} bits (Assumption 2.5 with ρ \rho the position-averaged prefix law of P P ) gives ψ = 4096 ​ ε ≈ 4.1 \psi=4096\,\varepsilon\approx 4.1 bits over 4096 4096 tokens, enough to degrade every task by four bits. At prior mass λ = 2 − k \lambda=2^{-k} , the certificate log ⁡ ( λ / t − ​ ( λ , ψ ) ) \log(\lambda/t^{-}(\lambda,\psi)) of clause (i) on in-context regret in excess of the Bayes mixture’s has leading term ψ ​ 2 k + 1 / ln ⁡ 2 \sqrt{\psi\,2^{k+1}/\ln 2} bits while ψ ≪ 2 − k \psi\ll 2^{-k} and is nearly ψ ​ 2 k \psi\,2^{k} beyond. Computed exactly, for a best-case ψ = 10 − 3 \psi=10^{-3} bits per window it is 2.14 2.14 bits at k = 10 k=10 , where ψ ​ 2 k ≈ 1 \psi\,2^{k}\approx 1 lies between the two regimes and the leading term reads 1.72 1.72 , and 1050 1050 bits at k = 20 k=20 ; at ψ ≈ 4.1 \psi\approx 4.1 bits it is 4.2 × 10 3 4.2\times 10^{3} bits already at k = 10 k=10 . The certificate is exponentially weak in k k , where Solomonoff’s guarantee is linear. Third, a split of ψ \psi into prior error and within-task misfit exists, but it depends on a convention (Proposition E.3 ).

sections.heading: Steering by demonstrations.
sections.text: The same posterior that makes in-context learning work makes a Bayes mixture steerable, quantitatively (Proposition D.10 ): if every demonstration multiplies each competitor’s likelihood ratio by at most 2 − r 2^{-r} , the served continuation law is within total variation η \eta of the target hypothesis h y h_{y} once the number of demonstrations reaches ( log ⁡ ( 1 / w h y ) + log ⁡ ( 1 / η ) ) / r (\log(1/w_{h_{y}})+\log(1/\eta))/r . A matching necessary length holds for concentration of the posterior. Choosing the demonstrations on which a model is least confident, as Wan and Mei propose [ 188 ] , is what the proposition already favours, since steering speed is set by the per-demonstration evidence rate r r , largest where hypotheses disagree; no Solomonoff approximation is needed for it. That many-shot jailbreaking [ 3 ] works by this mechanism is a hypothesis, supported by the fit of Bayesian scaling laws to many-shot curves [ 5 ] . Wolf et al. [ 195 ] are the direct antecedent. In a mixture model of behaviours, any behaviour of positive prior weight can be elicited by a prompt whose length grows with the logarithm of the inverse weight. The defence this suggests is dogmatism about designated behaviours imposed on the predictive distribution (a zero prior weight alone does not suffice, since other hypotheses can reproduce the excluded one; Section 9.3 ), and it is not what post-training is known to do: safety alignment can be shallow, concentrated in the first few output tokens [ 153 ] . Non-dogmatism about the world entails steerability by whoever controls the context, whenever demonstrations carry evidence at a positive rate against every competitor (Proposition D.10 ; Section 9.3 ).

sections.heading: Tools, retrieval and test-time compute.
sections.text: A tool or retriever combined with the model as a joint mixture keeps each component’s bound at the cost of its weight, while interpolation of conditionals and selection between them need not; and extra computation at test time changes what the model computes, not the prior it holds. Appendix D.4 gives the statements.

sections.heading: 7 Asymptotic criteria cannot see allocation
sections.text: The conclusions that universal approximation and a strictly proper loss can deliver are asymptotic: consistency, merging, vanishing per-step excess loss over the source. The classical Bayesian versions of these properties hold for every prior that gives the truth positive weight. Doob’s consistency theorem [ 39 ] , merging of opinions [ 14 ] and weak merging [ 98 ] all have this character. They are also weaker than they sound in the other direction: Doob’s theorem exempts a null set of parameters, and [ 36 ] show the exemption can bite, exhibiting priors with full support under which the posterior concentrates on the wrong answer. Consistency is therefore cheap in both senses: it holds for almost any prior that covers the truth, and where it fails it fails without warning. This strengthens rather than weakens the reading below: a criterion that almost every prior satisfies cannot distinguish among priors, and failing it does not single out any prior either. Solomonoff’s guarantee is a statement about constants. The elementary results below (formal statements in Appendix C.5 ) make precise why a property invariant under finite modification and reweighting cannot entail a bound that both operations destroy.

sections.heading: Tail invariance.
sections.text: Let q ′ q^{\prime} agree with q q outside a finite set F F of contexts, and let both have all conditionals on F F at least γ > 0 \gamma>0 . For F = 𝒜 < N F=\mathcal{A}^{<N} this constant is N N rather than ( V N − 1 ) / ( V − 1 ) (V^{N}-1)/(V-1) . Finite total regret, R n / n → 0 R_{n}/n\to 0 and vanishing per-step excess loss are therefore unchanged by any such modification; we call properties of this kind tail-invariant .

For every function f f , the property “ R ∞ ​ ( ⋅ , μ ) ≤ f ⁡ ( K ⁡ ( μ ) ) R_{\infty}(\cdot;\mu)\leq f(K(\mu)) for all computable μ \mu ” therefore fails for all large N N (Theorem C.9 ).

sections.heading: Prior-blindness.
sections.text: Tail invariance concerns finite modifications. Reweighting a prior is a second operation that asymptotic criteria cannot see. On the binary class of sequences z ( j ) := 0 j ​ 1 ∞ z^{(j)}:=0^{j}1^{\infty} , the Bayes mixture ( 2 ) has regret exactly log ⁡ ( 1 / w j ) \log(1/w_{j}) on z ( j ) z^{(j)} at every horizon n ≥ j + 1 n\geq j+1 . Its per-step excess loss is exactly zero after step j + 1 j+1 . Its constants can be set to f ⁡ ( j ) + j + 1 f(j)+j+1 for any prescribed f f (Proposition C.10 ; cf. [ 197 , 115 ] ). At n = ∞ n=\infty this is the attainment clause of Theorem 2.7 . For an arbitrary pairwise singular family the same holds along the whole frontier (Corollary C.11 ). All full-mass Bayes mixtures with positive weights, and their leaky variants, share every consistency property, while their regret profiles differ by unbounded amounts. Frontier membership is itself not tail-invariant: changing a frontier mixture’s conditional at a single context where some member charges every one-symbol continuation moves it strictly inside the Kraft set.

sections.heading: The implication in (C) is invalid.
sections.text: Combining these results gives Corollary C.12 . On any uniformly computable countable class of sources with a deterministic member, a consistency property satisfied by a computable Bayes mixture does not entail a complexity bound on that class for any f f . The finite- ε \varepsilon premise of Assumption 2.5 is not tail-invariant, but by Theorem 3.1 (ii) a modification on a set B B changes it by at most ρ ⁡ ( B ) ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / γ ) \rho(B)\log(1/\gamma) . Placing the uniform modification on the contexts of a simple deterministic environment, once that environment has left the region the corpus produces, gives the same separation at an ε \varepsilon -cost as small as log ⁡ V \log V times the ρ \rho -mass of those contexts. “Language models are, or approach, ε \varepsilon -optimal under the log-loss” does not entail “language models approach Solomonoff induction”, and the separating witnesses are computable and explicit.

sections.heading: In words.
sections.text: Consistency, merging and vanishing per-step divergence cannot distinguish Solomonoff’s predictor from one that learned nothing for its first N N steps. Nor can they distinguish two Bayesian predictors whose priors differ arbitrarily. What they cannot see is the allocation of the conserved budget.

sections.heading: 7.1 What “language models are Bayesian” can mean
sections.text:
Bayesian descriptions of in-context learning (Section 6.1 ) have also been tested on coin flips [ 69 ] and on flight and hotel recommendation, where Bayesian behaviour appears only after training on a Bayesian model’s predictions [ 154 ] . The results above constrain what such descriptions can carry, in three ways. First, “Bayesian” without a declared class and prior does not restrict a coherent model: every probability measure q q on 𝒜 ∞ \mathcal{A}^{\infty} is the integral mixture, with prior q q itself, of the point masses on sequences, and its conditionals are the corresponding posterior predictives. The content of the description lies in the declared class and in coherence, which Section 10 treats. Second, once a class is declared, every asymptotic signature of Bayesian behaviour is shared by all priors that give the truth positive weight (prior-blindness, above), so observing one identifies no prior, nor whether it came from data, architecture or post-training. Third, even the universal class does not fix a prior. Universal priors built from different reference machines agree only up to a multiplicative constant, and that constant is unbounded over machines, so at any finite horizon the choice of machine is unconstrained by the universality requirement; the class of universally dominant priors is in any case strictly larger than the Solomonoff–Levin constructions [ 197 ] . For agents, Leike and Hutter [ 115 ] show that a suitable choice of universal prior makes Legg–Hutter intelligence [ 112 ] , and with it balanced Pareto optimality, entirely subjective, and that every policy is Pareto optimal in the class of all computable environments. The elementary prediction analogue we use is not claimed there. For any computable measure ν 
u and δ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \delta\in(0,1) , the predictor ( 1 − δ ) ​ ν + δ ​ M (1-\delta)
u+\delta M dominates every lower-semicomputable semimeasure, so it is universal in the dominance sense of Fact 2.4 . Its regret exceeds ν 
u ’s by at most log ⁡ 1 1 − δ \log rac{1}{1-\delta} on every source, and exceeds Solomonoff’s bound by at most log ⁡ 1 δ \log rac{1}{\delta} (the argument of Theorem D.5 ). Every computable predictor is thus within log ⁡ 1 1 − δ \log rac{1}{1-\delta} bits of some universal predictor, which is weaker than being the posterior predictive of a universal prior but enough to make “universal” uninformative about behaviour. Taken together, these points mean that a claim that a model “is Bayesian”, or “approximately Solomonoff”, has empirical content only as a statement about constants over a declared class at finite horizon. Reading such constants from served conditionals is the subject of Section 10.3 .

sections.heading: 8 The deployed regime
sections.text: Sections 3 – 7 treat a model as one computable predictor on unbounded streams (Definition 2.2 ). A deployed model reads through a context window of W W tokens and is sampled at a temperature, often with truncation. It predicts tokens rather than characters, and it increasingly answers after a reasoning trace. This section says what each of these does to the preceding results.

sections.text: An unrestricted Bayes mixture pays once to identify the task, at most H ⁡ ( w ) H(w) bits (Proposition 8.1 (i)). A model that sees W W tokens cannot keep that identification; the proposition caps the cost and exhibits a source meeting the cap, but gives no general rate. The cap (ii): on stationary tasks the memory term grows at most at the identification cost plus the tasks’ excess entropy, divided by W + 1 W+1 , and linearly unless nothing beyond the window is there to be inferred. The witness (iii): ω W + 1 \omega_{W+1} is the uniform mixture of the V W + 1 V^{W+1} sequences of period W + 1 W+1 , of complexity at most log ⁡ W + O ⁡ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ W ) \log W+O(\log\log W) . An unrestricted predictor identifies the sequence once, for ( W + 1 ) ​ log ⁡ V (W+1)\log V bits; every window- W W predictor pays log ⁡ V \log V bits per token forever, the whole identification cost again every W + 1 W+1 tokens. On other stationary families the tax lies anywhere between zero and the cap. Evidence of in-context learning at lengths below W W is silent on this regime. sections.heading: Truncation, tokenisation and reasoning traces.
sections.text: Top- k k , top- p p and min- p p truncation, masks and majority votes are dogmatism by design: they give zero probability to every excluded continuation, so no bound survives on it. A tokeniser makes the read a marginal over tokenisations, and a reasoning trace makes the answer law a marginal over traces. Appendix F.5 gives the details and what each does to the properties of Section 9 .

sections.heading: What a served read reads.
sections.text: Serving stacks apply a checkpoint’s default truncation unless it is overridden, so a read must override it and say so. Commercial APIs return only top- k k log-probabilities, from which full conditionals could be recovered through logit bias on the API versions studied [ 52 , 19 ] ; providers have since restricted this. A server-side mask to an alphabet, renormalised step by step, is over the full vocabulary itself a truncation; over the alphabet the renormalised conditionals define a predictor, the one to which Assumption 10.1 is applied. It is neither the model’s own continuation law, which puts the discarded mass on other tokens, nor that law conditioned on staying in the alphabet, which would reweight each step by the probability that the rest of the continuation stays there. A read of this kind must state the mask, the serving configuration and the discarded mass; Paper B describes such reads.

sections.heading: 9 Properties ranked, and those to avoid
sections.text: Solomonoff’s predictor has a bundle of properties, of which universality is only one. This section separates them, ranks them by weight for trustworthiness, records which are attainable, and identifies those a deployed system should lack. The ranking is a judgement; the attainability column is not.

sections.heading: 9.1 Two floors
sections.text: Two properties, both attainable by computable systems, are floors: they say what a trustworthy inductor is never worse than. Definition 9.1 (Non-dogmatism, per environment) . A predictor q q is dogmatic on an environment z ∈ 𝒜 ∞ z\in\mathcal{A}^{\infty} if sup t − log q ( z t ∣ z < t ) = ∞ \sup_{t}-\log q(z_{t}\mid z_{<t})=\infty , and non-dogmatic on a class of environments if it is dogmatic on none of them. The quantifier matters: on a computable deterministic z z Solomonoff’s predictor pays at most K ⁡ ( z ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) K(z)+O(1) bits at any step (Fact 2.4 ), but along 0 t ​ 1 0^{t}1 its final surprisal is unbounded in t t , and a ceiling uniform over all environments would force linear loss on every deterministic stream. A Bayes mixture over a deterministic class has ceiling log ⁡ ( 1 / w h ) \log(1/w_{h}) on each member h h ; fixed share over m m experts, one of them uniform, with re-mixing rate α \alpha has ceiling log ⁡ ( m / α ) + log ⁡ V \log(m/\alpha)+\log V [ 75 ] ; truncated sampling fails the definition (Section 8 ). Dogmatism is unrecoverable: Bayesian updating cannot raise a zero. Definition 9.2 (Expert dominance) . A predictor q q dominates an expert p p with constant c c on a set X X of streams up to horizon n n if L n ′ ​ ( q , x ) ≤ L n ′ ​ ( p , x ) + c L_{n^{\prime}}(q;x)\leq L_{n^{\prime}}(p;x)+c for every x ∈ X x\in X and every n ′ ≤ n n^{\prime}\leq n . A Bayes mixture giving p p weight w p w_{p} dominates it with c = log ⁡ ( 1 / w p ) c=\log(1/w_{p}) (Fact D.3 ), and Solomonoff’s predictor dominates every computable expert with c ≤ K ⁡ ( p ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) c\leq K(p)+O(1) (Fact 2.4 ), in particular the Krichevsky–Trofimov (KT) estimator [ 109 ] ; linear excess over KT exposes a hole in the prior that the simplest expert fills. The floor has a bounded-window scope: a predictor that sees only the last W W symbols over an alphabet of V V has, on some i.i.d. source, per-step excess over KT tending to about ( V − 1 ) / ( 2 ​ W ​ ln ⁡ 2 ) (V-1)/(2W\ln 2) bits, the window tax of Proposition 8.1 for the i.i.d. family (Appendix G.3 ). A failure within the window shows that KT is not a component of any mixture the model implements over that horizon, not that the model is no mixture.

sections.heading: Calibration.
sections.text: A coherent predictor is calibrated exactly under its own law [ 33 ] and under an evaluation distribution only asymptotically; Solomonoff’s predictor is calibrated on computable environments in the limit [ 173 , 89 ] , a tail property with no constant (Fact C.8 ); Section 5 records what post-training costs in calibration, and calibration itself has a price in generation: a calibrated language model must hallucinate arbitrary facts at a rate close to the fraction of such facts seen once in training [ 97 ] .

C.3 ; [ 197 ] none a For the semimeasure M M , after normalisation. b Of a Bayes mixture over a class exchangeable (respectively closed under relabelling, with invariant prior) for the task; not of M M . Table 1: Properties of Solomonoff’s predictor, ranked by weight for trustworthiness. A property ranks higher the more its failure lets a user be misled or exploited without a visible error. The properties that make an inductor safe to rely on (rows 1–6) are all attainable, expert dominance within the context window, while universality (row 11), which cannot be had, ranks near the bottom because trust does not require it. The constants that carry informative content (rows 4, 8, 9; Section 7 ) need log-probabilities, or temperature or logit-bias control, the rows with exact black-box nulls (1, 5, 6) are structural, and row 10, often invoked as evidence of inductive quality, carries none. A ranking of the ideal’s properties should say where the ideal itself fails, and both of its documented failures are failures of the budget it leaves unspent. Solomonoff’s predictor converges to every computable μ \mu with μ \mu -probability one, which is a statement about sources and not about individual sequences: [ 88 ] show that some universal semimeasures fail to converge on some μ \mu -Martin-Löf random sequences, while certain non-universal ones converge on all of them. And when only selected positions carry structure (the even bits of a sequence whose odd bits are noise), [ 110 ] show that the normalised predictor M norm M_{\mathrm{norm}} still learns any recursive pattern on the selected positions, whereas M M itself can fail on very simple ones. That is the allocation thesis of § 2.3 turned on M M : what M M leaks is budget not placed on the continuations that are scored, and renormalising puts it back, which is what sampling at temperature one serves (Corollary 8.2 ). Universality buys a constant against every computable source; what it buys at a place of the examiner’s choosing depends on where the rest of the budget goes.

sections.heading: 9.3 Properties that are undesirable in deployment
sections.text: Solomonoff induction is an ideal of belief formation about a fixed world. A deployed system must also hold constraints, adapt to change and resist manipulation, and each of these is served by violating one property of the table, so a recommendation to make systems “more Solomonoff-like” is underspecified until it says which properties, for which role.

sections.heading: Non-dogmatism is steerability.
sections.text: A Bayes mixture is steered towards any hypothesis of positive weight by demonstrations (Section 6 , Proposition D.10 ). The defence is deliberate dogmatism about designated hypotheses, imposed on the predictive distribution. A zero prior weight does not suffice, because other hypotheses can reproduce the excluded one. By the conservation law (Section 2.2 ), this dogmatism only moves budget away from environments one never wishes to predict.

sections.heading: Occam allocation and corpus-optimality are choices.
sections.text: Simplicity weighting suits low-complexity environments, and its premium over a trained model is small only under the conditions of Section 5 . A perfect corpus predictor is the corpus law (Theorem 5.1 ), and so, on our reading, reproduces the corpus’s errors and harms at corpus rates; post-training departs from the corpus law on purpose, at the costs recorded there.

sections.heading: Exchangeability is the absence of an instruction hierarchy.
sections.text: Order invariance is desirable where demonstrations are conditionally i.i.d. by specification (Proposition 10.3 ). In a conversation position is informative: the system prompt should dominate the user turn, which is why an instruction hierarchy is trained explicitly [ 187 ] .

sections.heading: Beliefs and constraints.
sections.text: The properties that remain desirable without condition are the structural ones: coherence, the dominance floor within the window, and non-dogmatism about the world. The rest are desirable for beliefs and harmful for constraints, or right for a fixed world and wrong for a drifting one (bounded reversal is inertia after a regime change, which fixed share [ 75 ] escapes at a tracking cost), and each has the helpful violation named above. Our position, motivated but not proved by the results, is that a trustworthy system has Solomonoff-like beliefs and non-Solomonoff-like constraints. Solomonoff induction is silent about objectives: the properties ranked here are epistemic hygiene, the part of reliability that is a measurement problem.

sections.heading: 10 What served conditionals determine
sections.text: Tail-invariant statistics cannot see the constants (Section 7 ), and statistics on a fixed evaluation distribution cannot see allocation off it (Theorem 3.1 ). Merging of opinions is invariant under both (Appendix G.2 ). What remains readable is coherence, invariance, constants against explicit reference values, and the prior over a declared class. This section states these as definitions and identities; estimators, noise floors and validation are in Paper B.

sections.heading: 10.1 Elicitation and coherence
sections.text: Assumption 10.1 (Elicitation) . The served probability of an event A A at history h h equals the probability of A A under the served model’s own continuation law from h h , both read at T = 1 T=1 , without truncation (top- k k , top- p p , min- p p , grammar masks, server-side defaults included) and on one fixed tokenisation. (For a masked read, the served model is the masked, per-step renormalised predictor of Section 8 . Log-probabilities that the serving stack returns before temperature scaling count as a read at T = 1 T=1 , whatever temperature the request carries; log-probabilities returned before masking read the unmasked model, and renormalised over the allowed symbols they give the masked predictor’s conditionals. Whether a stack returns raw or processed values must be checked and stated.) The assumption is substantive: prompted probabilities differ from direct measurements [ 85 ] , answers depend on prompt format [ 165 ] , and a law on symbols is a marginal over tokenisations (Section 8 ), so a character-level residual may come from the tokeniser unless each symbol is one token. For post-trained models verbalised confidence can be better calibrated than token probabilities [ 179 ] , so a report must state which served object is read. Proposition 10.2 (Coherence and arbitrage; (ii)–(iii) after de Finetti [ 34 ] ) . Let Q Q be the served conditionals and A A an event determined by the continuation of h h . (i) (Null.) If some probability measure has conditionals agreeing with Q Q on { h } ∪ { h ​ σ : σ ∈ 𝒜 } \{h\}\cup\{h\sigma:\sigma\in\mathcal{A}\} and assigns A A the served values, then ϱ ⁡ ( h , A ) := | Q ⁡ ( A ∣ h ) − ∑ σ ∈ 𝒜 Q ⁡ ( σ ∣ h ) ​ Q ​ ( A ∣ h ​ σ ) | = 0 . \varrho(h;A)\;:=\;\Bigl|Q(A\mid h)-\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{A}}Q(\sigma\mid h)\,Q(A\mid h\sigma)\Bigr|\;=\;0. (6) So ϱ ⁡ ( h , A ) > 0 \varrho(h;A)>0 excludes every measure, hence every Bayes mixture under every prior on every machine, and for an autoregressive model it refutes Assumption 10.1 ; for the semimeasure M M the null holds after normalisation. (ii) (Arbitrage.) Let served conditionals be prices at which the system takes either side of unit claims on A A and on the next symbol, at h h and every h ​ σ h\sigma . The portfolio that buys, for each σ \sigma , Q ⁡ ( A ∣ h ​ σ ) Q(A\mid h\sigma) units of the σ \sigma -claim at h h and, if σ \sigma occurs, one A A -claim at h ​ σ h\sigma with the proceeds synthesises the A A -claim without refunds. Traded against the direct claim, it pays a riskless profit ϱ ⁡ ( h , A ) \varrho(h;A) per unit. (iii) (Converse.) If all served prices are probabilities of one measure, no riskless portfolio exists; ϱ ≡ 0 \varrho\equiv 0 for one event is necessary for this, not sufficient. (Proof: Appendix G.1 .) Under a masked read, a positive residual refutes Assumption 10.1 for the masked, renormalised predictor, not for the model’s unmasked continuation law.

sections.heading: Reading budget statistics against the floor.
sections.text: With a reference mixture P ref P_{\rm ref} over a task family, L n ( Q ; z 1 : n ) = log ( P ref ( z 1 : n ) / Q ( z 1 : n ) ) − log P ref ( z 1 : n ) L_{n}(Q;z_{1:n})=\log\bigl(P_{\rm ref}(z_{1:n})/Q(z_{1:n})\bigr)-\log P_{\rm ref}(z_{1:n}) , pathwise regret plus the reference’s own cost. On many distinct deterministic tasks the second term is bounded below by the Kraft floor of Section 2.2 for every predictor, so raw budgets should be reported net of − log ⁡ P ref -\log P_{\rm ref} , or beside its distribution.

sections.heading: 10.3 Reading the prior
sections.text: “The model’s prior” exists only relative to a declared class, even within the universal class (Section 7.1 ). Given the class, reading the prior is an inverse problem. Iterated in-context learning, which feeds a model’s answers back to it as data, samples a model’s prior over a task’s answers [ 207 ] ; the reading here instead fixes a declared class and inverts served probabilities.

sections.text: Claim (C) would require a computable system to hold Solomonoff’s allocation, and the known results show that none can. That is not a failure of the training objective: what it does not fix is the hypothesis class and the prior, and by the conservation law (Section 2.2 ) allocation, and how much of the budget is used, are all there is to fix (the ledger of Proposition B.2 ). sections.heading: The weaker forms, revisited.
sections.text: Figure 1 records what survives of each weaker form. The compression view’s strongest evidence lies off the corpus: a text-trained model compresses image patches and audio in context better than PNG and FLAC, on 2048-byte chunks [ 37 ] . Such a rate certifies no constant on a declared class (Theorem 3.1 ). Whether it beats an adaptive low-order context model (context-tree weighting [ 194 ] , PPM) on the same chunks is not reported by Delétang et al. [ 37 ] and, to our knowledge, not since [ 78 ] . If it does, the network’s allocation on data its pretraining law barely charges goes beyond what in-context adaptive coding obtains; if not, the rate is explained by it. Pretraining loss leaves that allocation almost free: Proposition 6.1 (i) at small prior mass, or (iii) at disjoint support. There the simplicity-bias form applies [ 182 , 136 , 62 ] , and meta-learned predictors [ 63 , 142 ] are uncertified; which prior a trained network holds is an empirical question for Section 10 and Paper B.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: The Kraft-sum reading of the frontier is exact only for mutually singular families (Theorem 2.7 ). For finite overlapping families the achievable region is known (the overlapping frontier, Proposition B.4 (i)); for countable non-singular families only C ∞ > 1 C_{\infty}>1 is proved (Proposition B.2 (ii)), and the achievable region and the maximising priors are open. The window, temperature, post-training and corpus statements concern idealised objects (window- W W predictors, exact tempering, the exact KL-regularised optimiser at a fixed prompt, a corpus as a task mixture). Checks on known systems and served-model readings are Paper B’s. The readings of Section 10.3 remove the declared prior but not the declared class, which is the irreducible residue of any measurement of a model’s prior.

sections.heading: What the measurements show.
sections.text: Paper B [ 210 ] carries these instruments to served models: a panel of twenty-six checkpoints of several pre-training families, sizes, architectures and serving precisions, each read as a predictor over a three-symbol alphabet through a bare-digit rendering, restricted to the digits and renormalised step by step, with eight re-read under a second rendering. Three of its findings bear on the argument here. The served conditionals put mass on continuations that no member of the declared class produces, as any model not confined to the class must (Proposition 10.5 ). No checkpoint’s median stays within the 3.32 3.32 bits by which a mixture carrying the Krichevsky–Trofimov code at weight 0.10 0.10 can trail it (the best trails it by 4.5 4.5 bits, the median by 36.5 36.5 and the worst by 128 128 at twenty-four symbols), but over 256 256 symbols the three nearest that bound settle to seven to thirteen bits, as a mixture carrying the code at a smaller weight would, while three others keep losing ground; the ordering of these distances also follows the mass each model puts outside the alphabet, so how much of it belongs to the checkpoint is open. And the reading closest to Solomonoff’s allocation, a model’s position between an enumerated mixture and a complexity-blind anchor, tracks, except in one family, the mass the model puts off the alphabet and moves with the rendering, so no effect of scale on allocation is established; read as a semimeasure, as M M is, with the leaked mass counted as loss, the high-leak checkpoints nearest the Krichevsky–Trofimov code on the class fall to the middle of the panel. Separately, the serving floor of a served model’s readings spans a factor of seventy-five across the panel, is predicted on the second engine neither by weight precision nor by architecture, and depends on the rendering, which is why each reading is certified against its own serving floor. These are measurements of particular deployments under stated renderings, not theorems. They are consistent with the division argued here: mixture-like behaviour on a declared class, with constants that differ by model, is measurable in served models, while their allocation is not yet separable from the interface through which it is read.

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: What language models can inherit from Solomonoff induction is not its allocation: no computable model holds it, and none of the routes offered for (C), whether evaluation, scale, corpus fit or asymptotic criteria, could establish that one does. What they can inherit is its form on declared classes: Bayes mixtures attain Solomonoff-form guarantees there, and a pretraining loss certifies in-context constants on a task family only through that family’s prior mass. Because every predictor spends the same Kraft budget, the questions that remain are where a given model spends it and which Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have: Solomonoff-like beliefs under non-Solomonoff-like constraints. On a declared class, coherence residuals, invariance nulls and the implied prior read that allocation from served conditionals, and a companion paper turns them into tests with exact nulls. What those tests report of any particular deployment is that paper’s to establish and not this one’s; what this paper establishes is that, on a declared class, the allocation is the quantity that carries Solomonoff’s guarantee and that no asymptotic criterion can see it. Whether a given read measures the model’s allocation rather than its interface is an empirical question, and the companion finds it confounded, under the renderings it reads, with the mass the model puts outside the alphabet.
