sections.heading: Accuracy and fidelity are distinct coordinates.
sections.text: An accuracy score is a coarse function of a model’s conditionals, and the two can come apart. Take P ∗ P^{*} to be the conditionals of an exhaustively enumerated reference mixture and let the evaluation be an answer-accuracy benchmark. Corollary C.1 then says that passing at any accuracy level is compatible with near-maximal disagreement with that reference on every context of a set of mass δ \delta , at resolution N ​ δ N\delta . A dissociation of this kind, high answer accuracy alongside distributional fidelity below the reference, is observed in companion work [ 49 ] . Where a served model exposes sampled text but not token log-probabilities, fidelity to a reference can only be estimated from samples, at the costs analysed in Paper B. Emergent abilities, which appear as sudden jumps in task metrics with scale [ 191 ] , are a second instance. Schaeffer et al. [ 160 ] show that many such jumps are artefacts of discontinuous metrics applied to smoothly improving per-token likelihoods. In the terms above, the jump is a property of the verdict map, not of the conditionals, and conversely a smooth metric can hide large changes in the conditionals off the evaluated set.

sections.heading: Red teaming falsifies but does not certify.
sections.text: Red teaming, whether by people [ 56 ] , by other language models [ 148 ] , or by gradient-guided search for adversarial suffixes [ 208 ] , is an adaptive protocol in the sense of Theorem C.2 . A failure it finds falsifies agreement. A campaign that finds none bounds disagreement only on sets carrying a large share of its query mass: evidence about the searched region, not a certificate for the contexts deployment will produce.

sections.heading: Scaling laws measure ε \varepsilon on ρ \rho .
sections.text: Under the log-loss, the population loss on the corpus prefix law is the source’s conditional entropy plus the averaged divergence of Assumption 2.5 . Scaling laws fit held-out loss as power laws in parameters, data and compute [ 99 ] . The parametric fit of Hoffmann et al. [ 82 ] separates an irreducible term from reducible terms that fall with parameters and training tokens. The fitted irreducible term is a power-law asymptote, not a measured source entropy, and its fitted value is sensitive to the fitting procedure [ 10 ] ; data-constrained laws keep it fixed and let repetition discount the effective data terms [ 137 ] . If it is read as the source’s entropy, the reducible part is the per-token ε \varepsilon , with ρ \rho the corpus prefix law, and a better scaling curve shrinks ε \varepsilon . By Theorem 3.1 (i), the resulting control over a set of contexts degrades as ε / ρ ⁡ ( B ) \varepsilon/\rho(B) , and it says nothing where ρ \rho puts no mass. No value of ε \varepsilon closes this gap (Section 4 ), and the asymptotic conclusions a vanishing ε \varepsilon supports cannot see allocation (Section 7 ).

sections.heading: Contamination.
sections.text: Theorem 3.1 (iii) assumes that the model is fixed independently of the probe draws. Contamination breaks that assumption. A model that has been trained on a benchmark’s items is the modification of clause (ii) run in reverse, with agreement placed on exactly the queried set, and its score certifies nothing off that set. Memorisation of training sequences is measurable and grows with scale [ 18 ] . Oren et al. [ 141 ] detect contamination without access to training data by exchangeability: an uncontaminated model has no reason to prefer a benchmark’s canonical item order over random permutations, the order-invariance null of Proposition 10.3 used in reverse. Dynamic and continually refreshed benchmarks [ 102 ] restore independence by drawing probes after the model is fixed. An evaluation that is to bear on inductive claims should therefore report its probe distribution, its resolution 1 / N 1/N , whether the protocol was fixed before the model, and whether conditionals were read or sampled (Section 11 ).

sections.heading: The family diagonal has no force on any particular model at an observable horizon.
sections.text: Because ( d i ) (d_{i}) is nonincreasing and summable, d i ≤ 1 / i d_{i}\leq 1/i . Clause (i) therefore forces a loss on member i i only at horizons beyond 4 ​ i 4i . A concrete model of 10 11 10^{11} bits sits at an index of order 2 10 11 2^{10^{11}} in any enumeration of such models ordered by description length; an enumeration that lists it early buys force on that model only, which is Theorem 4.1 again. The environment μ ∗ \mu^{*} thus forces nothing on it at any horizon that will ever be observed. The caveat applies to every statement below about “all models”: Theorem C.7 concerns families and the quantifier exchange discussed next. The result with force on a given model is Theorem 4.1 , together with its resource-bounded form (Section 8 ). Subject to that caveat, every concrete transformer language model whose decoding loop runs under an enforced step clock is a member of one such family, and so defeated by one fixed sequence (Corollary C.4 ). The clock is needed because a budget bounded only by some computable function cannot be checked from a description, and so cannot be enumerated.

sections.heading: Pointwise versus uniform: the quantifier exchange.
sections.text: Solomonoff’s property has the form “there is a predictor that, for every environment and every horizon, pays a bounded constant”. The evidence from scaling has the form “for every environment and horizon that we test, there is a model in the family that does well”. Here the model depends on the horizon. Theorem C.7 shows that the second form is compatible with the failure of the first on one fixed environment of constant complexity. Every finite benchmark, on every distribution and at every horizon n n , is consistent with late members performing excellently, μ ∗ \mu^{*} included, while every fixed member eventually has linear regret on μ ∗ \mu^{*} . How late “late” is depends on the schedule, which the adversary chooses: for any computable nondecreasing n ⁡ ( i ) n(i) with ∑ i 1 / n ⁡ ( i ) ≤ 1 \sum_{i}1/n(i)\leq 1 , d i = 1 / n ⁡ ( i ) d_{i}=1/n(i) defeats member i i beyond horizon 4 ​ n ​ ( i ) 4n(i) . Scaling curves [ 99 , 82 ] are evidence for the pointwise form on ρ \rho . A better curve shrinks ε \varepsilon and leaves Theorems 4.1 and C.9 untouched. Nor does passing to the limit help. M M ’s conditional is Δ 2 0 \Delta^{0}_{2} [ 114 ] : limit-computable, so computable families converging pointwise to it exist, and pointwise convergence is not what fails. What fails is selection: a rule that selects, ensembles, anneals or switches between members by any computable function of the data is itself one computable predictor, with its own diagonal, so no computable rule can tell at a finite stage which member to use, and a family approaches Solomonoff’s predictor only relative to an uncomputable selection oracle.

sections.heading: Tools and retrieval.
sections.text: A pipeline that queries retrieval or tools satisfies Definition 2.2 only relative to what it queries, and the diagonal of Section 4 applies relative to the same resources. What remains is how components are combined, and the results distinguish three ways. • Mixture of joint laws. q δ = ( 1 − δ ) ​ q N + δ ​ q E q_{\delta}=(1-\delta)q_{N}+\delta q_{E} , with posterior-weighted conditionals, has regret at most min ⁡ { R n ​ ( q N , μ ) + log ⁡ 1 1 − δ , R n ​ ( q E , μ ) + log ⁡ 1 δ } \min\{R_{n}(q_{N};\mu)+\log\frac{1}{1-\delta},\,R_{n}(q_{E};\mu)+\log\frac{1}{\delta}\} on every environment (Corollary D.8 ). • Per-step interpolation. Interpolating conditionals at a fixed weight, as the kNN-LM does [ 101 ] and as RAG-Token does across retrieved documents [ 119 ] , loses that bound. Against a deterministic environment that one component predicts exactly, while the other keeps its conditionals at least γ \gamma , the regret grows linearly in n n (Corollary B.3 (iii)). RAG-Sequence, which marginalises documents over whole sequences, is a mixture of joint laws. • Selection. Routing a query to a tool and substituting its answer, as in learned tool use [ 162 ] , is a selector. A selector can trail its better component by an amount linear in n n (Remark D.9 gives an example). With q E q_{E} an enumerated mixture, q δ q_{\delta} carries certified constants on the class 𝒞 E \mathcal{C}_{E} and the network’s uncertified constants elsewhere, so its guarantee has two tiers and should be reported that way. The competence sets of the two components overlap: trained networks copy in context [ 139 ] , prefer simple sequences [ 62 ] , and extrapolate numeric sequences zero-shot [ 67 ] . So the gain is a certificate on a declared class, not new coverage of a disjoint region. There is no gain in depth: on every string the mixture is no better than its better component.

sections.heading: Test-time compute.
sections.text: Chain of thought and search leave the end-to-end map computable, so they do not escape the diagonal. They change which resource-bounded class a model can cover, at a cost of enumeration exponential in the description length S S (Section 8 , Appendix I ).

sections.heading: Setting.
Post-training reallocates.
sections.text: At a fixed prompt and horizon, the exact maximiser of a KL-regularised reward objective is a Gibbs tilt of the pretrained law [ 106 , 155 ] . By the post-training identity (Remark E.5 ), the tilt changes the regret on each environment by an affine function of that environment’s mean reward, a price no KL budget bounds, and it is a change of prior over a task family, a move along the Kraft frontier at horizon n n , iff the reward is almost surely constant within every task (for tasks singular at horizon n n ). Practical PPO and DPO runs do not reach this optimiser. If one reward on complete strings (prompt and response together) and one coefficient β \beta are used at every prompt, the exact per-prompt optimisers are conditionals of one joint tilt. The objective itself, and not just optimisation and serving, can make a post-trained model incoherent only when the reward or the coefficient depends on where the prompt/response boundary falls: a reward that scores the response alone, or a prompt-dependent β x \beta_{x} with one complete-string reward. Best-of- n n sampling and reward-model reranking are tilts by a monotone transform of the reward (for best-of- n n with a continuous reward the density ratio to the base law is n ​ F ​ ( r ) n − 1 nF(r)^{n-1} , F F the reward’s distribution function under the base law), so the affine identity applies with the transformed reward in place of r r . Best-of- n n stays within ln ⁡ n − ( n − 1 ) / n \ln n-(n-1)/n nats of the base law in KL [ 8 ] , and as a proxy reward is optimised the gold reward eventually falls, with a KL dependence fitted by simple functional forms [ 57 ] .

sections.heading: Data mixing and refitting.
sections.text: For sources singular at the horizon (disjoint supports over the window), doubling a source of weight w < 1 2 w<\frac{1}{2} buys exactly one bit on it and costs exactly log ⁡ 1 − w 1 − 2 ​ w \log\frac{1-w}{1-2w} bits on each other source, about w ​ log ⁡ e w\log e for small w w ; repetition is the extreme case of up-weighting (the data-mixture corollary, Corollary E.4 ). For overlapping sources log ⁡ ( 1 / w ) \log(1/w) is only an upper bound. About four epochs of repeated data are nearly as useful as fresh data, and further repetition is worth ever less [ 137 ] . Maximum-likelihood refitting on generated data keeps the Kraft sum at one while the allocation drifts to a vertex (Proposition E.6 , for known components singular at the horizon and refits of the weights only), the absorbing chain noted by Shumailov et al. [ 167 ] .

sections.heading: Calibration after post-training.
sections.text: The visible cost of reallocation is calibration. The GPT-4 base model is well calibrated on a multiple-choice benchmark, while the post-trained model is markedly less so [ 140 ] . Kadavath et al. find RLHF policies miscalibrated until the temperature is raised to about 2.5 2.5 [ 95 ] , and output diversity falls after RLHF [ 103 ] . Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards raises pass@1, while the base model reaches higher pass@ k k at large k k [ 202 ] : probability moves onto rewarded solutions and away from others the base model could sample, a direct instance of reallocation. By Corollary A.3 , if post-training gains b b bits on every rewarded solution in a set A A of base mass q ⁡ ( A ) q(A) , the post-trained model keeps at most 1 − 2 b ​ q ​ ( A ) 1-2^{b}q(A) of its mass elsewhere: for q ⁡ ( A ) = 0.2 q(A)=0.2 and b = 2 b=2 , 0.2 0.2 against 0.8 0.8 before. This is an illustration, consistent in direction with the pass@ k k loss at large k k rather than derived from it. Ouyang et al. report a benchmark “alignment tax” [ 143 ] , and Bai et al. helpfulness–harmlessness trade-offs [ 6 ] . None of this is anomalous under the affine price, and calibration under the model’s own law (Section 9.1 ) is calibration against a reallocated law. Reading a served post-trained model therefore reads a post-trained allocation, not the pretraining prior, and a report should state which kind of checkpoint it reads (Paper B reads post-trained and base checkpoints; Section 8 ).

sections.heading: Stationarity is needed.
sections.text: With W = 1 W=1 , V = 2 V=2 , X 1 , X 2 X_{1},X_{2} uniform, X 3 := X 1 X_{3}:=X_{1} and later symbols i.i.d. uniform, the source is not 1 1 -Markov, yet its memory term is 1 1 bit at every n ≥ 3 n\geq 3 , so the dichotomy fails. The cap fails on the same source, and for the reason the proof identifies: its conditional entropies h ⁡ ( j ) h(j) run 1 , 1 , 0 , 1 , 1 , … 1,1,0,1,1,\dots , so the gaps h ⁡ ( j ) − h h(j)-h are not nonincreasing, the formal excess entropy is negative, and the right-hand side of (ii) falls below the memory term. Stationarity is therefore load-bearing for both halves of (ii), not only for the dichotomy.

sections.heading: Bounded recurrent state.
sections.text: If the conditional at time t t depends on the past only through a recurrently updated state of b b bits, then R n ​ ( q , ω ℓ ) ≥ ⌊ ( n − ℓ ) / ℓ ⌋ ​ ( ℓ ​ log ⁡ V − b ) + R_{n}(q;\omega_{\ell})\geq\lfloor(n-\ell)/\ell\rfloor\,(\ell\log V-b)^{+} , the log-loss form of the copying bound of [ 93 ] . On ℓ \ell consecutive steps after time ℓ \ell the truth’s loss is 0 0 , and the predictor’s expected loss is at least the entropy of the block given the state at their start, which is at least ℓ ​ log ⁡ V − b \ell\log V-b . A window is a state of W ​ log ⁡ V W\log V bits, for which this gives log ⁡ V \log V per period rather than per step.

sections.heading: F.4 Tokenisation
Truncation is dogmatism by design.
sections.text: Top- k top k_{\mathrm{top}} truncation to fewer than V V symbols assigns probability zero to some symbol at every context. So does top- p p truncation with threshold p top p_{\mathrm{top}} whenever V ≥ 1 / ( 1 − p top ) V\geq 1/(1-p_{\mathrm{top}}) (Proposition F.4 ), and so do min- p p , grammar masks and rounding to zero whenever they are active. Greedy decoding, the limit T → 0 T\to 0 , is top- 1 1 truncation. Read as a predictor, a truncated sampler has infinite regret at the first step on every source of full support and infinite loss on its own diagonal: the extreme form of the dogmatism excluded by Definition 9.1 . Nucleus sampling was introduced because sampling from the unreliable tail degrades text [ 83 ] , Hewitt et al. read truncation as undoing the model’s smoothing [ 79 ] , and the softmax bottleneck forces spurious nonzero tail mass, which truncation removes [ 51 ] . These readings agree with this one: truncation trades any guarantee on improbable continuations for sample quality on probable ones; under a softmax bottleneck the model cannot represent true near-zeros, so non-dogmatism and tail accuracy conflict, and truncation chooses the latter [ 51 ] . Non-dogmatism itself is cheap: smoothing any predictor to a floor ϕ \phi costs at most n ​ log ⁡ 1 1 − ( V − 1 ) ​ ϕ ≈ n ⁡ ( V − 1 ) ​ ϕ ​ log ⁡ e n\log\frac{1}{1-(V-1)\phi}\approx n(V-1)\phi\log e bits on any stream, and no floor can cost less on a deterministic one (Proposition F.4 ). For logits soft-capped at 30 30 with V = 2 18 V=2^{18} , the smallest probability representable is ϕ = 1 / ( 1 + ( V − 1 ) ​ e 60 ) ≈ 3 × 10 − 32 \phi=1/(1+(V-1)e^{60})\approx 3\times 10^{-32} , and a floor of that size costs about 10 − 26 10^{-26} bits per step, and the capped softmax itself pays at least 3 × 10 − 21 3\times 10^{-21} bits per step. The floor caps every single-step surprisal at about 105 105 bits, so a measured surprisal above that ceiling indicates truncation or numerics, not beliefs. A majority vote over N N sampled answers puts probability zero on every answer but the most frequent, whatever mass the model gives the rest. Training on truncated samples makes these zeros part of the next model’s allocation; Appendix E treats refitting on generated data.

sections.heading: Tokenisation.
sections.text: A language model is a measure over token sequences absent truncation, and a distribution over finite token strings only under tight end-of-sequence handling (Section 2.1 ). A claim about induction on text concerns the law over characters, which is the marginal over all tokenisations of a string [ 17 , 151 , 183 ] . By Proposition F.5 , the marginal is a semimeasure (a measure if the token law is one) and dominance constants pass through marginalisation, so Solomonoff’s guarantee is tokeniser-invariant up to O ⁡ ( K ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) ) O(K(\mathcal{A})) bits. Scoring only the canonical tokenisation instead gives a semimeasure that loses the model’s mass on non-canonical token strings, and dominance does not pass through it. That mass is reported to be small for trained models [ 17 , 24 ] . Still, models generate non-canonical token sequences [ 23 ] , aggregating over non-canonical tokenisations carries signal [ 59 ] , and conditioning on a canonically tokenised prompt can give probability zero to continuations of positive marginal probability [ 149 , 150 ] : a failure of non-dogmatism created by the interface, not by the beliefs. How digits are tokenised alone changes arithmetic accuracy sharply [ 169 ] . For the programme of Section 10.3 , a character-level coherence residual can come from the tokeniser alone, and a slope of surprisal against description length includes the tokeniser’s own allocation. Rendering each symbol as a single token (for example digits, under a tokeniser that splits digits individually) removes this confound, but not a second one: a read restricted to the alphabet and renormalised discards the mass the model puts elsewhere, and what is discarded depends on the rendering; the rendering and the discarded mass must be stated for each model.

sections.heading: Chain of thought, test-time compute and effective context.
sections.text: When a model answers after a reasoning trace ζ \zeta , its answer law is ∑ ζ p ⁡ ( ζ ∣ x ) ​ p ​ ( a ∣ x , ζ ) \sum_{\zeta}p(\zeta\mid x)\,p(a\mid x,\zeta) , a marginal over traces. This has three consequences. Reading. No single log-probability gives this law; reading it requires sampling traces, self-consistency voting [ 190 ] estimates its mode, and Assumption 10.1 applies to the marginal. Compute. Deployed models have finite description length and bounded computation per emitted symbol. Chain of thought and search leave the end-to-end map a closed computable predictor with a larger per-step budget, so the diagonals of Section 4 apply unchanged; they use nothing beyond computability. What changes is the class the pipeline can cover end to end. The per-step computation of a fixed-depth, log-precision transformer lies within uniform TC 0 \mathrm{TC}^{0} [ 132 ] ; with polynomially many reasoning steps, transformers reach exactly polynomial time [ 133 ] , chain of thought lets constant-size transformers solve arithmetic and dynamic-programming tasks they cannot solve directly [ 48 ] , and test-time compute can substitute for parameters [ 171 ] . Architectures also differ in the classes on which they generalise: on formal-language tasks, structured memory generalises higher in the Chomsky hierarchy, while transformers fail on some regular tasks [ 35 ] , an empirical counterpart of a class. Appendix I states both diagonals in the resource-bounded regime on one reference machine, with the following consequences. Let 𝒞 V ​ ( S , τ ) \mathcal{C}_{V}(S,\tau) be the class of sequences generated by programs of at most S S bits within time τ ⁡ ( n ) \tau(n) at step n n . • A clocked Bayes mixture has regret at most S S bits on every member of 𝒞 V ​ ( S , τ ) \mathcal{C}_{V}(S,\tau) , at per-symbol time about 2 S + 1 ​ n ​ τ ​ ( n ) 2^{S+1}n\,\tau(n) , exponential in the description length S S . • A predictor program p p with per-step time t p t_{p} loses at least n ​ ⌊ log ⁡ V ⌋ n\lfloor\log V\rfloor in n n steps on a diagonal environment in 𝒞 V ​ ( | p | + c 0 , τ ) \mathcal{C}_{V}(|p|+c_{0},\tau) whenever τ \tau exceeds t p t_{p} by a quasi-linear simulation overhead. The uniform version has a rate exponentially small in the model’s first-step time, so at deployed sizes it is qualitative only. • Whether the exponential factor is necessary is open. Per-step and total compute thus decide which class 𝒞 V ​ ( S , τ ) \mathcal{C}_{V}(S,\tau) a system covers, not whether it has a diagonal: the environment on which it fails moves with the budget. Test-time compute is how a fixed model buys coverage, at up to the enumeration price. Context. Nominal and effective context differ. Models use information in the middle of long contexts poorly [ 121 ] , and long-context benchmarks find effective lengths well below the nominal ones [ 84 ] . Weak use of distant information is not a hard window: Proposition 8.1 applies with W W the nominal window, since only beyond it is information provably discarded. Reading W W as the effective context is an analogy, not a consequence of the proposition: by it the tax, and the horizons over which the floors of Section 9 and Paper B’s tests can be read, would be bounded by effective context, which is not proved here.

(iii) If Q Q gives positive probability to a continuation no hypothesis allows, ℒ = ∞ \mathcal{L}=\infty for all w w ; a full-support column makes it finite and absorbs the off-class mass. ∎

sections.heading: Merging is free.
sections.text: Merging of opinions [ 14 ] , like any observed per-step excess tending to 0 0 , is invariant under finite modification (Fact C.8 ) and prior reweighting (Proposition C.10 ): evidence of coverage, never of good coverage.

sections.heading: G.3 The window excess over KT
sections.text: Let Θ \Theta have Jeffreys’ prior on the V V -symbol simplex, with X 1 , X 2 , … X_{1},X_{2},\dots i.i.d. given Θ \Theta . sections.heading: G.4 A corpus as one hypothesis
sections.text: A corpus supplies the exact likelihood of one hypothesis, text drawn from its law μ \mu , with prefix probabilities from a certified model ( n n -gram, PPM or context-tree). With the column μ ⁡ ( c ) \mu(c) added to finitely many alternative columns, inverting as in Proposition G.1 recovers w μ Q w^{Q}_{\mu} , the model’s weight on corpus text before any context ( 1 1 for the perfect corpus predictor, Theorem 5.1 ), but neither a prior over English nor structure within μ \mu ; statistics on it belong to Paper B. Paper B checks the membership residual, the corpus weight and distillation on known reference systems.

sections.heading: Frontier.
sections.text: Proposition B.4 (i), with Pareto-optimal implying Bayes, is Wald’s complete-class theorem [ 186 , 15 ] , uniqueness coming from strict propriety of the log-loss; Pareto optimality of Bayes mixtures in sequence prediction is Hutter’s [ 87 ] . The compensation identity is Topsøe’s [ 180 ] , and the diagonal of (i) is the redundancy–capacity theorem [ 55 , 158 , 32 ] , with minimax theorems at n = ∞ n=\infty [ 170 , 71 ] . Not found stated: C n = 2 max λ H λ ( κ ∣ X 1 : n ) C_{n}=2^{\max_{\lambda}H_{\lambda}(\kappa\mid X_{1:n})} , whose maximisers follow from Csiszár–Tusnády optimal pairs [ 31 ] ; overlap bounds are of Kailath and Hellman–Raviv type [ 96 , 73 ] .

sections.heading: Resource bounds.
sections.text: Theorem I.4 (i) is the Putnam–Legg diagonal with time-hierarchy bookkeeping and simulation overhead [ 70 , 74 ] . Failure on sequences of slightly larger time bound is implicit in time-bounded randomness, resource-bounded measure and dimension [ 164 , 104 , 125 , 2 , 126 , 81 ] , where diagonalising against all n k n^{k} -time predictors, as in (ii), appears with exponential slowdown. For (iii), mixture regret over deterministic experts is standard [ 185 , 21 ] , clocked enumeration is AIXI t ​ l tl [ 89 , Ch. 7] and universal search [ 116 ] , and speed-prior prediction [ 163 ] is exponential- but not polynomial-time on polynomial-time sequences [ 50 ] . Added: a per-symbol two-sided statement on one class with explicit constants; the exponential gap is open.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: The loss identity behind Proposition E.1 is the posterior-predictive divergence of prior-data fitted networks [ 138 ] with Topsøe’s identity [ 180 ] . Zhang et al. bound in-context regret by a coverage constant (our 1 / λ 1/\lambda ) times pretraining error [ 204 ] , and Wies et al. need a floor on component weights [ 193 ] ; added are log-loss constants with equality case and sharpness. For post-training, the Gibbs identity underlies DPO [ 155 ] and the Bayesian reading is Korbak et al.’s [ 106 ] ; the frontier criterion and the Jensen-gap ledger are new. Minimax data mixtures are the redundancy–capacity theorem [ 55 , 32 , 130 ] , worst-case weighting is DoReMi [ 200 ] , and refitting as an absorbing chain with Wright–Fisher fixation is in [ 167 , 45 ] (kept real data change the dynamics [ 9 ] ); only the frontier reading is added.

sections.heading: Deployment.
sections.text: The window theorem is the relative-entropy chain rule plus the redundancy–capacity decomposition: summed stationary memory terms are the excess entropy [ 30 ] , the cap is Sharan et al.’s bound [ 166 ] in stationary form for mixtures, and the copy witness is folklore (bounded state: [ 93 ] ); not found stated are the memory term as the exact window tax and the dichotomy. For temperature, miscalibration is [ 68 ] , generalised-Bayes tempering acts on posterior weights [ 65 ] , and the 2 − K ⁡ ( t ) 2^{-K(t)} rate follows from dominance (cf. [ 89 ] ). Smoothing floors are standard [ 75 ] ; truncation and its desmoothing reading are [ 83 , 79 ] ; tokenisation marginals and bias are studied in [ 17 , 24 , 183 , 151 , 149 , 150 ] . The companion work [ 20 ] is in preparation; nothing here depends on it.

Limits, Attainable Properties, and What Served Conditionals Reveal Luan Ozelim Affiliation: Algocyte | Oxford Immune Algorithmics, Oxford University Innovation& London Institute for Healthcare Engineering, UK Abicumaran Uthamacumaran Affiliation: Algocyte | Oxford Immune Algorithmics, Oxford University Innovation& London Institute for Healthcare Engineering, UK Hector Zenil Affiliation: Algocyte | Oxford Immune Algorithmics, Oxford University Innovation& London Institute for Healthcare Engineering, UK Affiliation: Algorithmic Dynamics Lab, Department of Biomedical ComputingSchool of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, King’s Institute for AI,King’s College London, UK Abstract A familiar line of reasoning runs as follows: language models are flexible approximators trained under a strictly proper loss, so scale brings them closer to Solomonoff induction, and their predictive success is evidence of that approach. We apply known results from algorithmic information theory, universal prediction and Bayesian consistency. In its uniform form the conclusion holds for no computable model: each has cheap environments it never learns, and every uniformly computable family of total predictors shares one on which each member fails beyond a horizon growing with its index, so “closer” can hold only pointwise, one environment at a time. Nor could the offered routes certify even that: finite evaluation cannot certify agreement on rarely reached contexts, perfect corpus fit selects the corpus law as prior, and asymptotic criteria cannot see the constants that carry Solomonoff’s guarantee. Our lens is the Kraft inequality read for predictors. Every model has at most the same budget of predictive success, so Solomonoff’s predictor, which leaves part of it unspent, differs from a language model not in having more of it but in where it spends it; on mutually singular families this is exact, and only full-mass Bayes mixtures reach the frontier. We then discuss what is inheritable, including in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference; what survives within a context window; which Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have or avoid; and what served conditionals determine. A closing table states what common practices certify and what to report. Tests are developed in a companion paper. 1 Introduction Language models are trained to minimise the log-loss, a strictly proper scoring rule [ 60 ] , and transformers are universal approximators of continuous sequence-to-sequence functions of fixed length on compact domains [ 203 ] . A familiar line of reasoning joins these facts: with enough data and compute, such a model approaches the predictor that learns every computable source, Solomonoff’s mixture over all computable hypotheses under a simplicity prior [ 172 , 173 ] , and its measured predictive success is evidence of that approach. We call this claim (C). Claim (C) is not a position anyone defends at full strength, and we do not attribute it to anyone. It is the common strengthening of a family of positions that are defended, stated at full strength so that the obstacles can be located: each obstacle below falls at a different point, and a claim held at half strength would hide which. The positions themselves are the target, and Figure 1 records for each one what survives and which result applies. The closest published statement of (C) itself, the hypothesis that transformers approximate Solomonoff induction better than any other extant sequence predictor [ 201 ] , is comparative and carries no guarantee. Deployed models, whose compute-efficient training stops well short of convergence [ 99 , 82 ] , give (C) little direct purchase. The weaker forms identify language modelling with compression [ 37 ] , whose efficiency is reported to track benchmark performance almost linearly [ 86 ] ; credit networks with a simplicity bias matched to real data [ 62 , 136 ] ; report that neural predictors meta-trained on samples from a universal prior show falling regret with scale on such samples, with convergence to Solomonoff’s predictor established in the limit under realisability rather than demonstrated [ 63 ] ; or describe language models as computable approximations to Solomonoff induction [ 188 ] . Each is a statement about where a model predicts well, and each survives this paper in part. What does not survive is the step they can be read as licensing: that the part which survives certifies the rest. None of the results below says that such success is no evidence at all about allocation elsewhere; they say that no finite amount of it can guarantee that allocation. Compression efficiency tracking benchmark performance is a statement about a corpus and bears on no other allocation (§ 5 ); a simplicity bias matched to real data is a statement about one prior and not about a universal one (§ 6 ); falling regret on samples from a universal prior is convergence under realisability , which is the hypothesis at issue (§ 4 ); and a computable approximation to Solomonoff induction is what Section 4 shows cannot be uniform. Figure 1 states this position by position. The four positions, and what survives each. Compression. Language modelling is compression, and compression efficiency is reported to track capability [ 37 , 86 ] ; its most quoted informal statement in machine learning casts unsupervised learning as compression [ 177 ] . The position long predates that evidence. Compression on a fixed corpus was proposed as an objective replacement for the Turing test [ 127 ] , is the basis of a standing prize for compressing a snapshot of Wikipedia [ 90 ] , and was folded into formal intelligence measures by [ 76 , 77 ] ; the older form is the more specific one, because it names the corpus and so concedes what the recent form leaves open. A rate measures allocation on the data compressed , where universality costs at most K ⁡ ( q ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) K(q)+O(1) bits. What it does not do is certify a constant on a declared class: a rate below PNG or FLAC says nothing about one, and whether these models beat an adaptive low-order context model on the same chunks is not reported [ 37 , 78 ] . Compression by the shortest generated program, the reading closest to K K , remains far from strong baselines on real data [ 105 ] . Non-vacuous generalisation bounds do hold, on the training law and with prediction smoothing [ 122 , 123 ] . Survives as a statement about one corpus (§ 5 , Theorem 3.1 ). Simplicity bias. Networks prefer low-complexity functions and sequences, as real data do [ 62 , 136 ] . This is a direction of allocation, attainable and consistent with the no-free-lunch argument, and it is measurable as truth-loss levels on a declared class. What it is not is a universal prior, and asymptotic signatures cannot identify it (§ 6.1 , § 7 , Proposition 10.4 ). Meta-learned universal predictors. Neural predictors meta-trained on samples from a universal prior show falling regret with scale [ 63 ] , with convergence established in the limit under realisability rather than demonstrated. This is amortised Bayesian inference on the sampled class, certified in context by prior mass and exponentially weak in the task’s complexity. Outside the sampler’s bounds on program length and steps the prior is uncertified, and the network has its own diagonal environment (Proposition 6.1 , Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 ). Computable approximation. Training optimises program length through loss minimisation, and next-token prediction approximates Solomonoff induction better than other extant predictors [ 188 , 201 ] . The first reading is the K ⁡ ( q ) K(q) premium of § 5 : bounded and pathwise, but informative only where q q itself predicts well. Where a predictor spends the budget is what its prior is. Each obstacle to (C) below is a statement about allocation; where the lens is exact is stated in Section 2.3 (Figure 2 ). Contributions. This is a discussion paper: most individual results are known, the dozen or so new pieces are mostly elementary, and Appendix H gives the role of each. The terrain it crosses has a standard survey in [ 156 ] , which treats universal induction as a theory of inference and asks whether it is the right formalisation of Occam’s razor. The scope here is narrower in two ways. It is about prediction and not about agency: the universal-agent programme that extends Solomonoff induction with a utility and an action channel is out of scope, and where a result from it is used (Pareto optimality among predictors in § 2.3 ), it is used for its prediction half only. And the question is empirical rather than foundational: not whether Solomonoff induction is the right ideal, but which of its properties a trained and served language model can have, which it cannot, and which of the routes commonly offered for the claim that it approaches one could establish it. Item (ii) shows that the conclusion of (C) in its uniform form holds for no computable model, and that approach can hold only pointwise, and items (i), (iii) and (v) that no route offered for it could certify it. (i) Evaluation (Section 3 ). Near-optimal expected log-loss bounds divergence on a set of contexts only in inverse proportion to its probability, so N N queries, adaptive or not, cannot separate models that differ only where the queries rarely go. Benchmark and red-team evidence can falsify, but never certify, agreement with a reference, and scaling curves track the ε \varepsilon of the test distribution only. (ii) Scale (Section 4 ). Putnam’s diagonal [ 152 ] , in Legg’s form [ 113 ] , gives every computable model, closed pipelines with chain of thought included, an environment no more complex than itself on which it loses log ⁡ V \log V bits per step ( log ⁡ ( 2 ​ V / 3 ) \log(2V/3) for real-valued conditionals) while Solomonoff’s predictor pays a constant (for tools and retrieval see Section 2.1 ). A uniformly computable family of total predictors shares one such environment; this forces nothing on a given model at an observable horizon, but shows that apparent convergence along a scaling family rests on replacing “one model that is good at every horizon” by “at every horizon, some model that is good”. (iii) Data (Section 5 ). A predictor with zero regret on its corpus coincides with the corpus law, so has finite regret only on sources absolutely continuous with respect to it, and at most log ⁡ c \log c on those it dominates by c c : fitting a corpus chooses a prior. Solomonoff’s predictor pays at most K ⁡ ( q ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) K(q)+O(1) bits more than it on the corpus, below one percent of the corpus code length at about 2 2 bits per token, 16 16 -bit weights and at least 10 3 10^{3} tokens per parameter. Data curation and mixture weights are prior design, and post-training reallocates under the same budget. (iv) Inheritance (Section 6 ). Solomonoff-form guarantees are attainable on declared classes by Bayes mixtures, the formal content of in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference. We state what a pretraining loss certifies about the in-context allocation, and why demonstrations can steer it. (v) Asymptotics (Section 7 ). Consistency, merging and vanishing per-step excess loss survive finite modification and reweighting of the prior [ 14 , 197 , 115 ] , while Solomonoff’s guarantee lives in the constants these operations change. Such criteria are blind to the prior. (vi) Deployment (Section 8 ). Within a context window, conservation, underdetermination, the single diagonal and prior reading keep their force. On stationary sources a bounded-window model repays the cost of identifying its environment at most about once per window, and exactly that on a copy source; only temperature one keeps Solomonoff’s bound; truncation is dogmatism by design; and the character-level law is a marginal over tokenisations. (vii) Properties (Section 9 ). We record which “Solomonoff-like” properties are attainable and, as a judgement, rank them; several attainable ones are attack surfaces, and we argue, without proof, that a trustworthy system should have Solomonoff-like beliefs and non-Solomonoff-like constraints. (viii) Measurement (Section 10 ). We define what served conditionals determine without a prior: a coherence residual and the arbitrage it prices, invariance nulls, and the implied prior over a declared class with its identifiability. The companion paper (Paper B) [ 210 ] turns them into tests and applies them to served models. Section 11 draws the consequences for research practice. How to read this paper. Section 2 fixes notation and states the lens. Proofs are in the appendices, which open with a table of notation. Classical results are Facts, adapted or sharpened ones carry an “after” citation, and Appendix H records the status of each. Paragraphs headed “In words” restate key results. A shorter route for machine learning readers: Figure 1 , the Kraft lens (Section 2.2 and Figure 2 ), Sections 4 , 5 and 8 , and Table 2 . Resource-bounded forms of the limits are in Appendix I . What is claimed and what is not. Nothing below shows that language models generalise poorly, that scale is unproductive, or that any particular system is deficient: no computable system has the universal property, so impossibility is not deficiency. Nor is attainability universality (a system matching a declared posterior exactly has its own diagonal environment), or uncertifiability unmeasurability (coherence, invariance and a prior over a declared class remain measurable). The claims concern what a class of arguments can establish and a class of measurements can certify, for idealised predictors at stated horizons, and Section 8 says which survive deployment. The paper measures no language model of its own; the served-model readings it relays in Section 11 are Paper B’s and are labelled as such. Every predictor has the same fixed amount of predictive success to distribute over the strings of each length; predictors differ in where they put it and how much they leave unused, never in how much they have. On language models, accuracy on deterministic tasks tracks the probability of the output and of the task (rot-13 against rot-2), which is where the budget is spent [ 128 ] . The counting is that behind incompressibility; the correspondence between codes and priors it expresses underlies minimum description length and universal prediction [ 7 , 66 , 21 ] , and no-free-lunch results state the same trade for problems weighted uniformly [ 161 , 196 ] , which a simplicity prior escapes [ 111 ] . Whether that escape leaves the no-free-lunch theorems with any force against a learner that is doing well in practice is contested, and [ 174 ] argue the negative: the theorems presuppose learning algorithms that are purely data-driven, whereas standard algorithms take a model as input and can be given a model-relative justification, so the theorems constrain less than they are usually taken to. The counting used here does not depend on that dispute, and the difference is worth stating because the lens’s force rests on it. A no-free-lunch theorem averages performance over a weighting of problems and concludes that the average is fixed; change the weighting and the conclusion moves. The Kraft bound assumes no weighting at all. It says that on any antichain of strings (of one length, or any prefix-free set) at most 2 b 2^{b} members can be given loss below b b , because their probabilities must sum to at most one. That is a counting fact about the code, true of every predictor including M M , and it survives any reweighting of which problems matter. The simplicity prior escapes the average but not the ledger. Benchmarks draw prompts from a fixed distribution, red teams choose prompts adaptively, and scaling studies fit held-out loss curves. Two elementary tools, Markov’s inequality and a coupling of evaluation runs, show what this evidence can establish. It constrains a model’s conditionals only on contexts that the evaluation reaches with probability comparable to the inverse of its number of queries. It can therefore falsify agreement with a reference such as Solomonoff’s predictor, but it cannot certify that agreement where agreement would matter.
